cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: What is environmental pollution?
cards.back: Environmental pollution results from the release of substances and energy from waste products of human activities.
cards.quote: Environmental pollution results from the release of substances and energy from waste products of human activities.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Types of pollution, classified on the basis of the medium of transport and diffusion.
cards.back:
air pollution
water pollution
land pollution
noise pollution
cards.quote: Pollution can be classified into (i) air pollution, (ii) water pollution, (iii) land pollution and (iv) noise pollution.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the natural sources of water pollutants.
cards.back:
erosion
landslides
decay and decomposition of plants and animals
cards.quote: Though water pollutants are also created from natural sources (erosion, landslides, decay and decomposition of plants and animals, etc.) pollutants from human activities are the real causes of concern.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Through which activities do human beings pollute water?
cards.back:
industrial
agricultural
cultural activities
cards.quote: Human beings pollute the water through industrial, agricultural and cultural activities.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Table 9.1: sources of water pollution.
cards.back:
Sewage disposal
urban run-off
toxic effluents from industries
run-off over cultivated lands and nuclear power plants
cards.quote: Sewage disposal, urban run-off, toxic effluents from industries, run-off over cultivated lands and nuclear power plants.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Table 9.1: sources of land pollution.
cards.back:
Improper human activities
disposal of untreated industrial waste
use of pesticides and fertilisers
cards.quote: Improper human activities, disposal of untreated industrial waste, use of pesticides and fertilisers.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Table 9.1: sources of noise pollution.
cards.back:
Aircrafts
automobiles
trains
industrial processing
advertising media
cards.quote: Aircrafts, automobiles, trains, industrial processing and advertising media.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the major water polluting industries.
cards.back:
leather
pulp and paper
textiles
chemicals
cards.quote: Major water polluting industries are leather, pulp and paper, textiles and chemicals.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Which chemicals used in modern agriculture generate pollution?
cards.back:
inorganic fertilisers
pesticides
herbicides
cards.quote: Various types of chemicals used in modern agriculture such as inorganic fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides are also pollution generating components.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Fertiliser induces an increase in the ____ content of surface waters.
cards.back: Fertiliser induces an increase in the nitrate content of surface waters.
cards.quote: Fertiliser induces an increase in the nitrate content of surface waters.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the cultural activities that also cause water pollution.
cards.back:
pilgrimage
religious fairs
tourism
cards.quote: Cultural activities such as pilgrimage, religious fairs, tourism, etc. also cause water pollution.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the diseases commonly caused by contaminated water.
cards.back:
diarrhoea
intestinal worms
hepatitis
cards.quote: The diseases commonly caused due to contaminated water are diarrhoea, intestinal worms, hepatitis, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: What share of communicable diseases in India is water-borne, according to the WHO?
cards.back: about one-fourth
cards.quote: The World Health Organization shows that about one-fourth of the communicable diseases in India are water-borne.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the objectives of the Namami Gange Programme.
cards.back:
developing sewerage treatment systems in towns
monitoring of industrial effluents
development of river front
afforestation along the bank to increase biodiversity
cleaning of the river surface
development of 'Ganga Grams' in Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal
creating public awareness to avoid adding pollutants into the river even in the form of rituals
cards.quote: developing sewerage treatment systems in towns, monitoring of industrial effluents, development of river front, afforestation along the bank to increase biodiversity, cleaning of the river surface, development of 'Ganga Grams' in Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal, and creating public awareness to avoid adding pollutants into the river even in the form of rituals.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: What is air pollution?
cards.back: Air pollution is taken as addition of contaminants, like dust, fumes, gas, fog, odour, smoke or vapour to the air in substantial proportion and duration that may be harmful to flora and fauna and to property.
cards.quote: Air pollution is taken as addition of contaminants, like dust, fumes, gas, fog, odour, smoke or vapour to the air in substantial proportion and duration that may be harmful to flora and fauna and to property.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the main sources of air pollution.
cards.back:
Combustion of fossil fuels
mining
industries
cards.quote: Combustion of fossil fuels, mining and industries are the main sources of air pollution.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Which substances do combustion of fossil fuels, mining and industries release?
cards.back: oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, hydrocarbons, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, lead and asbestos
cards.quote: release oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, hydrocarbons, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, lead and asbestos.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Air pollution causes diseases related to which three systems?
cards.back: respiratory, nervous and circulatory systems
cards.quote: Air pollution causes various diseases related to respiratory, nervous and circulatory systems.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Smoky fog over cities called as urban ____ is caused by atmospheric pollution.
cards.back: Smoky fog over cities called as urban smog is caused by atmospheric pollution.
cards.quote: Smoky fog over cities called as urban smog is caused by atmospheric pollution.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Air pollution can also cause ____ rains.
cards.back: Air pollution can also cause acid rains.
cards.quote: Air pollution can also cause acid rains.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Rainwater analysis of urban environment has indicated that pH value of the first rain after summer is always ____ than the subsequent rains.
cards.back: Rainwater analysis of urban environment has indicated that pH value of the first rain after summer is always lower than the subsequent rains.
cards.quote: Rainwater analysis of urban environment has indicated that pH value of the first rain after summer is always lower than the subsequent rains.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: What is noise pollution?
cards.back: Noise pollution refers to the state of unbearable and uncomfortable to human beings which is caused by noise from different sources.
cards.quote: Noise pollution refers to the state of unbearable and uncomfortable to human beings which is caused by noise from different sources.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the main sources of noise pollution.
cards.back:
various factories
mechanised construction and demolition works
automobiles and aircraft
cards.quote: The main sources of noise pollution are various factories, mechanised construction and demolition works, automobiles and aircraft, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: The level of steady noise is measured by sound level expressed in terms of ____ (dB).
cards.back: The level of steady noise is measured by sound level expressed in terms of decibels (dB).
cards.quote: The level of steady noise is measured by sound level expressed in terms of decibels (dB).

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: What is solid waste?
cards.back: Solid waste refers to a variety of old and used articles, for example stained small pieces of metals, broken glassware, plastic containers, polythene bags, ash, floppies, CDs, etc., dumped at different places.
cards.quote: Solid waste refers to a variety of old and used articles, for example stained small pieces of metals, broken glassware, plastic containers, polythene bags, ash, floppies, CDs, etc., dumped at different places.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the two sources from which solid waste is disposed of.
cards.back:
household or domestic establishments
industrial or commercial establishments
cards.quote: These discarded materials are also termed as refuse, garbage and rubbish, etc., and are disposed of from two sources : (i) household or domestic establishments, and (ii) industrial or commercial establishments.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: How are household wastes and industrial solid wastes disposed off?
cards.back: The household wastes are disposed off either on public lands or on private contractors' sites, whereas the solid wastes of industrial units are collected and disposed off through public (municipal) facilities at low lying public grounds (landfill areas).
cards.quote: The household wastes are disposed off either on public lands or on private contractors' sites, whereas the solid wastes of industrial units are collected and disposed off through public (municipal) facilities at low lying public grounds (landfill areas).

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the diseases carried by flies and rodents harboured by solid wastes.
cards.back:
typhoid
diphtheria
diarrhoea
malaria
cholera
cards.quote: Solid wastes cause health hazard through creation of obnoxious smell, and harbouring of flies and rodents, which act as carriers of diseases like typhoid, diphtheria, diarrhoea, malaria and cholera, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: About what per cent of solid waste is collected and disposed in Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru?
cards.back: about 90 per cent
cards.quote: In metropolitan cities like Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, etc., about 90 per cent of the solid waste is collected and disposed.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: In most other cities and towns of India, what share of waste generated is left uncollected?
cards.back: about 30 to 50 per cent
cards.quote: But in most of other cities and towns in the country, about 30 to 50 per cent of the waste generated are left uncollected

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Untreated wastes ferment slowly and release toxic biogas to the atmosphere, including ____.
cards.back: Untreated wastes ferment slowly and release toxic biogas to the atmosphere, including methane.
cards.quote: Untreated wastes ferment slowly and release toxic biogas to the atmosphere, including methane.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Which universal law guided the effort to restore ecology at Daurala near Meerut?
cards.back: "Polluter pays"
cards.quote: Based on the universal law "Polluter pays", effort to restore the ecology and safeguard the human health with people's participation has taken place in Daurala near Meerut.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Rural-to-urban flow is caused by high demand for labour in urban areas and which two other factors?
cards.back:
low job opportunities in rural areas
unbalanced pattern of development between urban and rural areas
cards.quote: labour in urban areas, low job opportunities in rural areas and unbalanced pattern of development between urban and rural areas.
cards.note: Three factors: high demand for labour in urban areas, few rural jobs, unbalanced development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the ways in which urban population grows.
cards.back:
natural increase (when birth rate exceeds death rate)
net inmigration (when people move in than out)
reclassification of urban areas to encompass formerly rural population settlements
cards.quote: Urban population grows as a result of natural increase (when birth rate exceeds death rate), net inmigration (when people move in than out), and sometimes reclassification of urban areas to encompass formerly rural population settlements.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Why are spouses of rural-urban migrants left behind in rural areas?
cards.back: Since wages are very low to support the family at the place of destination, the spouses are left behind in rural areas to look after children and elderly people.
cards.quote: Since wages are very low to support the family at the place of destination, the spouses are left behind in rural areas to look after children and elderly people.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Who inhabits slums and jhuggi-jhopari clusters in urban centres?
cards.back: These are inhabited by those people who were forced to migrate from the rural areas to these urban centres in search of livelihood but could not afford proper housing due to high rent and high costs of land.
cards.quote: These are inhabited by those people who were forced to migrate from the rural areas to these urban centres in search of livelihood but could not afford proper housing due to high rent and high costs of land.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: What are slums?
cards.back: Slums are residential areas of the least choice, dilapidated houses, poor hygienic conditions, poor ventilation, lack of basic amenities, like drinking water, light and toilet facilities, etc.
cards.quote: Slums are residential areas of the least choice, dilapidated houses, poor hygienic conditions, poor ventilation, lack of basic amenities, like drinking water, light and toilet facilities, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Name the serious health and socio-environmental hazards in slums.
cards.back:
Open defecation
unregulated drainage system
overcrowded narrow street patterns
cards.quote: Open defecation, unregulated drainage system and overcrowded narrow street patterns are serious health and socioenvironmental hazards.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: What is the aim of the Swachh Bharat Mission as part of the urban renewal mission?
cards.back: to improve the quality of life in urban slums
cards.quote: The Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) is part of the urban renewal mission launched by the Government of India to improve the quality of life in urban slums.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Poverty makes slum dwellers vulnerable to what?
cards.back:
drug abuse
alcoholism
crime
vandalism
escapism
apathy
social exclusion
cards.quote: The poverty makes them vulnerable to drug abuse, alcoholism, crime, vandalism, escapism, apathy and ultimately social exclusion.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: What is land degradation?
cards.back: Land degradation is generally understood either as a temporary or a permanent decline in productive capacity of the land.
cards.quote: Land degradation is generally understood either as a temporary or a permanent decline in productive capacity of the land.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Which centre has classified wastelands using remote sensing techniques?
cards.back: National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC)
cards.quote: National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) has classified wastelands by using remote sensing techniques

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Types of wastelands primarily caused by natural agents.
cards.back:
gullied /ravinous land
desertic or coastal sands
barren rocky areas
steep sloping land
glacial areas
cards.quote: There are a few types of wastelands such as gullied /ravinous land, desertic or coastal sands, barren rocky areas, steep sloping land, and glacial areas, which are primarily caused by natural agents.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Types of degraded lands caused largely by natural as well as human factors.
cards.back:
waterlogged and marshy areas
land affected by salinity and alkalinity
land with or without scrub
cards.quote: There are other types of degraded lands such as waterlogged and marshy areas, land affected by salinity and alkalinity and land with or without scrub, which have largely been caused by natural as well as human factors.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Types of wastelands caused by human action.
cards.back:
degraded shifting cultivation area
degraded land under plantation crops
degraded forests
degraded pastures
mining and industrial wastelands
cards.quote: There are some other types of wastelands such as degraded shifting cultivation area, degraded land under plantation crops, degraded forests, degraded pastures, and mining and industrial wastelands, are caused by human action.

cards.subject: geography
cards.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.unit: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
cards.front: Watershed Management Programmes acknowledge the linkage between land, water and ____
cards.back: Watershed Management Programmes acknowledge the linkage between land, water and vegetation
cards.quote: Watershed Management Programmes acknowledge the linkage between land, water and vegetation

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Whose works spelt out the idea of the quality of life as development in the late eighties and early nineties?
cards.back: The works of two South Asian economists, Mahbub-ul-Haq and Amartya Sen are important in this regard.
cards.quote: The works of two South Asian economists, Mahbub-ul-Haq and Amartya Sen are important in this regard.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Who introduced the concept of human development?
cards.back: The concept of human development was introduced by Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq.
cards.quote: The concept of human development was introduced by Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Define human development (Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq).
cards.back: Dr Haq has described human development as development that enlarges people's choices and improves their lives.
cards.quote: Dr Haq has described human development as development that enlarges people's choices and improves their lives.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The basic goal of development is to create conditions where people can live ____.
cards.back: The basic goal of development is to create conditions where people can live meaningful lives.
cards.quote: The basic goal of development is to create conditions where people can live meaningful lives.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: A meaningful life is not just a long one. It must be a life with some ____.
cards.back: A meaningful life is not just a long one. It must be a life with some purpose.
cards.quote: A meaningful life is not just a long one. It must be a life with some purpose.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What must people be able to do for a life to be meaningful?
cards.back:
be healthy
be able to develop their talents
participate in society
be free to achieve their goals
cards.quote: This means that people must be healthy, be able to develop their talents, participate in society and be free to achieve their goals.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Who created the Human Development Index, and when?
cards.back: Pakistani economist Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq created the Human Development Index in 1990.
cards.quote: Pakistani economist Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq created the Human Development Index in 1990.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What did Prof Amartya Sen see as the main objective of development?
cards.back: Nobel Laureate Prof Amartya Sen saw an increase in freedom (or decrease in unfreedom) as the main objective of development.
cards.quote: Nobel Laureate Prof Amartya Sen saw an increase in freedom (or decrease in unfreedom) as the main objective of development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the key areas in human development.
cards.back:
access to resources
health
education
cards.quote: Therefore, access to resources, health and education are the key areas in human development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the most important aspects of human development.
cards.back:
Leading a long and healthy life
being able to gain knowledge
having enough means to be able to live a decent life
cards.quote: Leading a long and healthy life, being able to gain knowledge and having enough means to be able to live a decent life are the most important aspects of human development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Why may people lack the capability and freedom to make even basic choices?
cards.back:
inability to acquire knowledge
material poverty
social discrimination
inefficiency of institutions
cards.quote: This may be due to their inability to acquire knowledge, their material poverty, social discrimination, inefficiency of institutions and other reasons.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Building people's ____ in the areas of health, education and access to resources is therefore, important in enlarging their choices.
cards.back: Building people's capabilities in the areas of health, education and access to resources is therefore, important in enlarging their choices.
cards.quote: Building people's capabilities in the areas of health, education and access to resources is therefore, important in enlarging their choices.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the four pillars of human development.
cards.back:
equity
sustainability
productivity
empowerment
cards.quote: the idea of human development is supported by the concepts of equity, sustainability, productivity and empowerment.

source.section: The Four Pillars of Human Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Define equity (a pillar of human development).
cards.back: Equity refers to making equal access to opportunities available to everybody.
cards.quote: Equity refers to making equal access to opportunities available to everybody.

source.section: The Four Pillars of Human Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Define sustainability (a pillar of human development).
cards.back: Sustainability means continuity in the availability of opportunities.
cards.quote: Sustainability means continuity in the availability of opportunities.

source.section: The Four Pillars of Human Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: To have sustainable human development, ____ must have the same opportunities.
cards.back: To have sustainable human development, each generation must have the same opportunities.
cards.quote: To have sustainable human development, each generation must have the same opportunities.

source.section: The Four Pillars of Human Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What does productivity mean as a pillar of human development?
cards.back: Productivity here means human labour productivity or productivity in terms of human work.
cards.quote: Productivity here means human labour productivity or productivity in terms of human work.

source.section: The Four Pillars of Human Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Ultimately, it is ____ who are the real wealth of nations.
cards.back: Ultimately, it is people who are the real wealth of nations.
cards.quote: Ultimately, it is people who are the real wealth of nations.

source.section: The Four Pillars of Human Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Define empowerment (a pillar of human development).
cards.back: Empowerment means to have the power to make choices.
cards.quote: Empowerment means to have the power to make choices.

source.section: The Four Pillars of Human Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: ____ and people-oriented policies are required to empower people.
cards.back: Good governance and people-oriented policies are required to empower people.
cards.quote: Good governance and people-oriented policies are required to empower people.

source.section: The Four Pillars of Human Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Types of approaches to human development.
cards.back:
The income approach
The welfare approach
Minimum needs approach
Capabilities approach
cards.quote: Some of the important approaches are: (a) The income approach; (b) The welfare approach; (c) Minimum needs approach; and (d) Capabilities approach (Table 3.1).
cards.note: Table 3.1 names the third approach 'Basic Needs Approach'.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the income approach to human development?
cards.back: This is one of the oldest approaches to human development. Human development is seen as being linked to income.
cards.quote: This is one of the oldest approaches to human development. Human development is seen as being linked to income.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Higher the level of ____, the higher is the level of human development.
cards.back: Higher the level of income, the higher is the level of human development.
cards.quote: Higher the level of income, the higher is the level of human development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the welfare approach to human development?
cards.back: This approach looks at human beings as beneficiaries or targets of all development activities.
cards.quote: This approach looks at human beings as beneficiaries or targets of all development activities.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which organisation initially proposed the basic needs approach?
cards.back: This approach was initially proposed by the International Labour Organisation (ILO).
cards.quote: This approach was initially proposed by the International Labour Organisation (ILO).

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the six basic needs identified in the basic needs approach.
cards.back:
health
education
food
water supply
sanitation
housing
cards.quote: Six basic needs i.e.: health, education, food, water supply, sanitation, and housing were identified.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the capability approach to human development (Prof. Amartya Sen)?
cards.back: This approach is associated with Prof. Amartya Sen. Building human capabilities in the areas of health, education and access to resources is the key to increasing human development.
cards.quote: This approach is associated with Prof. Amartya Sen. Building human capabilities in the areas of health, education and access to resources is the key to increasing human development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the human development index (HDI)?
cards.back: The human development index (HDI) ranks the countries based on their performance in the key areas of health, education and access to resources.
cards.quote: The human development index (HDI) ranks the countries based on their performance in the key areas of health, education and access to resources.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Between what values does a country's HDI score lie?
cards.back: These rankings are based on a score between 0 to 1 that a country earns from its record in the key areas of human development.
cards.quote: These rankings are based on a score between 0 to 1 that a country earns from its record in the key areas of human development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which indicator is chosen to assess health in the HDI?
cards.back: The indicator chosen to assess health is the life expectancy at birth.
cards.quote: The indicator chosen to assess health is the life expectancy at birth.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which indicators represent access to knowledge in the HDI?
cards.back: The adult literacy rate and the gross enrolment ratio represent access to knowledge.
cards.quote: The adult literacy rate and the gross enrolment ratio represent access to knowledge.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How is access to resources measured in the HDI?
cards.back: Access to resources is measured in terms of purchasing power (in U.S. dollars).
cards.quote: Access to resources is measured in terms of purchasing power (in U.S. dollars).

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What weightage does each dimension get in the HDI?
cards.back: Each of these dimensions is given a weightage of 1/3. The human development index is a sum total of the weights assigned to all these dimensions.
cards.quote: Each of these dimensions is given a weightage of 1/3. The human development index is a sum total of the weights assigned to all these dimensions.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Why is the HDI not the most reliable measure of human development?
cards.back: Yet it is not the most reliable measure. This is because it does not say anything about the distribution.
cards.quote: Yet it is not the most reliable measure. This is because it does not say anything about the distribution.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What does the human poverty index measure?
cards.back: The human poverty index is related to the human development index. This index measures the shortfall in human development.
cards.quote: The human poverty index is related to the human development index. This index measures the shortfall in human development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What does human geography study, as against physical geography?
cards.back: Physical geography studies physical environment and human geography studies “the relationship between the physical/natural and the human worlds, the spatial distributions of human phenomena and how they come about, the social and economic differences between different parts of the world”.
cards.quote: Physical geography studies physical environment and human geography studies “the relationship between the physical/natural and the human worlds, the spatial distributions of human phenomena and how they come about, the social and economic differences between different parts of the world”.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: As you know geography as a field of study is ____, ____, and ____.
cards.back: As you know geography as a field of study is integrative, empirical, and practical.
cards.quote: As you know geography as a field of study is integrative, empirical, and practical.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the elements of the physical environment.
cards.back:
landforms
soils
climate
water
natural vegetation
diverse flora and fauna
cards.quote: You know that these elements are landforms, soils, climate, water, natural vegetation and diverse flora and fauna.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Define human geography (Ratzel).
cards.back: “Human geography is the synthetic study of relationship between human societies and earth’s surface”.
cards.quote: “Human geography is the synthetic study of relationship between human societies and earth’s surface”.
cards.note: Synthesis is the emphasis in Ratzel's definition.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Define human geography (Ellen C. Semple).
cards.back: “Human geography is the study of the changing relationship between the unresting man and the unstable earth.”
cards.quote: “Human geography is the study of the changing relationship between the unresting man and the unstable earth.”

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: ____ in the relationship is the keyword in Semple’s definition.
cards.back: Dynamism in the relationship is the keyword in Semple’s definition.
cards.quote: Dynamism in the relationship is the keyword in Semple’s definition.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Define human geography (Paul Vidal de la Blache).
cards.back: “Conception resulting from a more synthetic knowledge of the physical laws governing our earth and of the relations between the living beings which inhabit it”.
cards.quote: “Conception resulting from a more synthetic knowledge of the physical laws governing our earth and of the relations between the living beings which inhabit it”.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Human beings interact with their physical environment with the help of ____.
cards.back: Human beings interact with their physical environment with the help of technology.
cards.quote: Human beings interact with their physical environment with the help of technology.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Natural laws and technology: what did friction and heat, DNA and genetics, and aerodynamics help humans do?
cards.back: For example, the understanding of concepts of friction and heat helped us discover fire. Similarly, understanding of the secrets of DNA and genetics enabled us to conquer many diseases. We use the laws of aerodynamics to develop faster planes.
cards.quote: For example, the understanding of concepts of friction and heat helped us discover fire. Similarly, understanding of the secrets of DNA and genetics enabled us to conquer many diseases. We use the laws of aerodynamics to develop faster planes.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The physical environment for such societies becomes the “____”.
cards.back: The physical environment for such societies becomes the “Mother Nature”.
cards.quote: The physical environment for such societies becomes the “Mother Nature”.

source.section: Naturalisation of Humans and Humanisation of Nature

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is possibilism?
cards.back: The earlier scholars termed this as possibilism. Nature provides opportunities and human being make use of these and slowly nature gets humanised and starts bearing the imprints of human endeavour.
cards.quote: The earlier scholars termed this as possibilism. Nature provides opportunities and human being make use of these and slowly nature gets humanised and starts bearing the imprints of human endeavour.

source.section: Naturalisation of Humans and Humanisation of Nature

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is neodeterminism (Griffith Taylor)?
cards.back: A geographer, Griffith Taylor introduced another concept which reflects a middle path (Madhyam Marg) between the two ideas of environmental determinism and possibilism. He termed it as Neodeterminism or stop and go determinism.
cards.quote: A geographer, Griffith Taylor introduced another concept which reflects a middle path (Madhyam Marg) between the two ideas of environmental determinism and possibilism. He termed it as Neodeterminism or stop and go determinism.

source.section: Naturalisation of Humans and Humanisation of Nature

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: In stop and go determinism, what do the red, amber and green lights mean?
cards.back: Red light means ‘stop’, amber light provides a gap between red and green lights ‘to get set’ and green light means ‘go’.
cards.quote: Red light means ‘stop’, amber light provides a gap between red and green lights ‘to get set’ and green light means ‘go’.

source.section: Naturalisation of Humans and Humanisation of Nature

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The concept shows that neither is there a situation of ____ (environmental determinism) nor is there a condition of ____ (possibilism).
cards.back: The concept shows that neither is there a situation of absolute necessity (environmental determinism) nor is there a condition of absolute freedom (possibilism).
cards.quote: The concept shows that neither is there a situation of absolute necessity (environmental determinism) nor is there a condition of absolute freedom (possibilism).

source.section: Naturalisation of Humans and Humanisation of Nature

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the results of the free run taken by the developed economies.
cards.back:
green house effect
ozone layer depletion
global warming
receding glaciers
degrading lands
cards.quote: The free run which the developed economies attempted to take has already resulted in the green house effect, ozone layer depletion, global warming, receding glaciers and degrading lands.

source.section: Naturalisation of Humans and Humanisation of Nature

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The neo-determinism conceptually attempts to bring a ____ nullifying the ‘either’ ‘or’ dichotomy.
cards.back: The neo-determinism conceptually attempts to bring a balance nullifying the ‘either’ ‘or’ dichotomy.
cards.quote: The neo-determinism conceptually attempts to bring a balance nullifying the ‘either’ ‘or’ dichotomy.

source.section: Naturalisation of Humans and Humanisation of Nature

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Welfare or humanistic school of thought in human geography was mainly concerned with the different aspects of ____ of the people.
cards.back: Welfare or humanistic school of thought in human geography was mainly concerned with the different aspects of social well-being of the people.
cards.quote: Welfare or humanistic school of thought in human geography was mainly concerned with the different aspects of social well-being of the people.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the aspects of social well-being the welfare (humanistic) school studied.
cards.back:
housing
health
education
cards.quote: These included aspects such as housing, health and education.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Radical school of thought employed ____ to explain the basic cause of poverty, deprivation and social inequality.
cards.back: Radical school of thought employed Marxian theory to explain the basic cause of poverty, deprivation and social inequality.
cards.quote: Radical school of thought employed Marxian theory to explain the basic cause of poverty, deprivation and social inequality.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Contemporary social problems were related to the development of ____.
cards.back: Contemporary social problems were related to the development of capitalism.
cards.quote: Contemporary social problems were related to the development of capitalism.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Behavioural school of thought laid great emphasis on ____ and also on the ____ by social categories based on ethnicity, race and religion, etc.
cards.back: Behavioural school of thought laid great emphasis on lived experience and also on the perception of space by social categories based on ethnicity, race and religion, etc.
cards.quote: Behavioural school of thought laid great emphasis on lived experience and also on the perception of space by social categories based on ethnicity, race and religion, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Human geography was made more relevant to the ____ by the emergence of these schools of thought.
cards.back: Human geography was made more relevant to the socio-political reality by the emergence of these schools of thought.
cards.quote: Human geography was made more relevant to the socio-political reality by the emergence of these schools of thought.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the sub-fields of Social Geography (Table 1.2).
cards.back:
Behavioural Geography
Geography of Social Well-being
Geography of Leisure
Cultural Geography
Gender Geography
Historical Geography
Medical Geography
cards.quote: Behavioural Geography Geography of Social Well-being Geography of Leisure Cultural Geography Gender Geography Historical Geography Medical Geography

source.section: Fields and Sub-fields of Human Geography

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the sub-fields of Political Geography (Table 1.2).
cards.back:
Electoral Geography
Military Geography
cards.quote: Electoral Geography Military Geography

source.section: Fields and Sub-fields of Human Geography

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the sub-fields of Economic Geography (Table 1.2).
cards.back:
Geography of Resources
Geography of Agriculture
Geography of Industries
Geography of Marketing
Geography of Tourism
Geography of International Trade
cards.quote: Geography of Resources Geography of Agriculture Geography of Industries Geography of Marketing Geography of Tourism Geography of International Trade

source.section: Fields and Sub-fields of Human Geography

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is a human settlement?
cards.back: Human Settlement means cluster of dwellings of any type or size where human beings live.
cards.quote: Human Settlement means cluster of dwellings of any type or size where human beings live.
cards.note: A human settlement is a cluster of dwellings, from a hamlet to a metropolis.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The sparsely located small settlements are called ____, specialising in agriculture or other primary activities.
cards.back: The sparsely located small settlements are called villages, specialising in agriculture or other primary activities.
cards.quote: The sparsely located small settlements are called villages, specialising in agriculture or other primary activities.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Rural vs urban settlements: the difference on economic base.
cards.back: The rural settlements derive their life support or basic economic needs from land based primary economic activities, whereas, urban settlements, depend on processing of raw materials and manufacturing of finished goods on the one hand and a variety of services on the other.
cards.quote: The rural settlements derive their life support or basic economic needs from land based primary economic activities, whereas, urban settlements, depend on processing of raw materials and manufacturing of finished goods on the one hand and a variety of services on the other.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Rural vs urban settlements: the difference on social relations and way of life.
cards.back: Rural people are less mobile and therefore, social relations among them are intimate. In urban areas, on the other hand, way of life is complex and fast, and social relations are formal.
cards.quote: Rural people are less mobile and therefore, social relations among them are intimate. In urban areas, on the other hand, way of life is complex and fast, and social relations are formal.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is a rather universal feature of rural settlement in India, particularly in the northern plains?
cards.back: In India compact or clustered village of a few hundred houses is a rather universal feature, particularly in the northern plains.
cards.quote: In India compact or clustered village of a few hundred houses is a rather universal feature, particularly in the northern plains.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where are semi-clustered settlements widespread in India?
cards.back: Such settlements are widespread in the Gujarat plain and some parts of Rajasthan.
cards.quote: Such settlements are widespread in the Gujarat plain and some parts of Rajasthan.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is a clustered rural settlement?
cards.back: The clustered rural settlement is a compact or closely built up area of houses.
cards.quote: The clustered rural settlement is a compact or closely built up area of houses.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where are clustered settlements generally found in India?
cards.back: Such settlements are generally found in fertile alluvial plains and in the northeastern states.
cards.quote: Such settlements are generally found in fertile alluvial plains and in the northeastern states.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where do people live in compact villages for security or defence reasons?
cards.back: Sometimes, people live in compact village for security or defence reasons, such as in the Bundelkhand region of central India and in Nagaland.
cards.quote: Sometimes, people live in compact village for security or defence reasons, such as in the Bundelkhand region of central India and in Nagaland.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Why has compact settlement become necessary in Rajasthan?
cards.back: In Rajasthan, scarcity of water has necessitated compact settlement for maximum utilisation of available water resources.
cards.quote: In Rajasthan, scarcity of water has necessitated compact settlement for maximum utilisation of available water resources.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is a hamleted settlement?
cards.back: Sometimes settlement is fragmented into several units physically separated from each other bearing a common name.
cards.quote: Sometimes settlement is fragmented into several units physically separated from each other bearing a common name.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What are the units of a hamleted settlement locally called?
cards.back: These units are locally called panna, para, palli, nagla, dhani, etc. in various parts of the country.
cards.quote: These units are locally called panna, para, palli, nagla, dhani, etc. in various parts of the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where are hamleted villages more frequently found?
cards.back: Such villages are more frequently found in the middle and lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh and lower valleys of the Himalayas.
cards.quote: Such villages are more frequently found in the middle and lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh and lower valleys of the Himalayas.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which areas of India have dispersed settlement?
cards.back: Many areas of Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Kerala have this type of settlement.
cards.quote: Many areas of Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Kerala have this type of settlement.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How does the Census of India, 1991 define urban settlements?
cards.back: The census of India, 1991 defines urban settlements as "All places which have municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee and have a minimum population of 5000 persons, at least 75 per cent of male workers are engaged in non-agriculture pursuits and a density of population of at least 400 persons per square kilometer are urban.
cards.quote: The census of India, 1991 defines urban settlements as "All places which have municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee and have a minimum population of 5000 persons, at least 75 per cent of male workers are engaged in non-agriculture pursuits and a density of population of at least 400 persons per square kilometer are urban.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the criteria of an urban place in the Census of India, 1991.
cards.back:
municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee
minimum population of 5000 persons
at least 75 per cent of male workers are engaged in non-agriculture pursuits
density of population of at least 400 persons per square kilometer
cards.quote: The census of India, 1991 defines urban settlements as "All places which have municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee and have a minimum population of 5000 persons, at least 75 per cent of male workers are engaged in non-agriculture pursuits and a density of population of at least 400 persons per square kilometer are urban.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which towns existed even at the time of the Indus valley civilisation?
cards.back: Even at the time of Indus valley civilisation, towns like Harappa and Mohanjodaro were in existence.
cards.quote: Even at the time of Indus valley civilisation, towns like Harappa and Mohanjodaro were in existence.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: There are number of towns in India having historical background spanning over ____ years. Most of them developed as ____ and ____ centres.
cards.back: There are number of towns in India having historical background spanning over 2000 years. Most of them developed as religious and cultural centres.
cards.quote: There are number of towns in India having historical background spanning over 2000 years. Most of them developed as religious and cultural centres.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name examples of ancient towns in India.
cards.back: Varanasi is one of the important towns among these. Prayag (Prayagraj), Pataliputra (Patna), Madurai are some other examples of ancient towns in the country.
cards.quote: Varanasi is one of the important towns among these. Prayag (Prayagraj), Pataliputra (Patna), Madurai are some other examples of ancient towns in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: About ____ of the existing towns have their roots in the medieval period. Most of them developed as headquarters of ____ and kingdoms.
cards.back: About 100 of the existing towns have their roots in the medieval period. Most of them developed as headquarters of principalities and kingdoms.
cards.quote: About 100 of the existing towns have their roots in the medieval period. Most of them developed as headquarters of principalities and kingdoms.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the important medieval fort towns of India.
cards.back: These are fort towns which came up on the ruins of ancient towns. Important among them are Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra and Nagpur.
cards.quote: These are fort towns which came up on the ruins of ancient towns. Important among them are Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra and Nagpur.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which trading ports did the Europeans first develop on coastal locations?
cards.back: Starting their foothold on coastal locations, they first developed some trading ports such as Surat, Daman, Goa, Pondicherry, etc.
cards.quote: Starting their foothold on coastal locations, they first developed some trading ports such as Surat, Daman, Goa, Pondicherry, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which town is cited as an example of towns based on modern industries evolved after 1850?
cards.back: Towns based on modern industries also evolved after 1850. Jamshedpur can be cited as an example.
cards.quote: Towns based on modern industries also evolved after 1850. Jamshedpur can be cited as an example.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name towns developed after independence as administrative headquarters and as industrial centres.
cards.back: After independence, a large number of towns have been developed as administrative headquarters, e.g., Chandigarh, Bhubaneswar, Gandhinagar, Dispur, etc., and industrial centres, such as Durgapur, Bhilai, Sindri, Barauni.
cards.quote: After independence, a large number of towns have been developed as administrative headquarters, e.g., Chandigarh, Bhubaneswar, Gandhinagar, Dispur, etc., and industrial centres, such as Durgapur, Bhilai, Sindri, Barauni.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the satellite towns developed around Delhi.
cards.back: Some old towns also developed as satellite towns around metropolitan cities, such as Ghaziabad, Rohtak, Gurugram around Delhi.
cards.quote: Some old towns also developed as satellite towns around metropolitan cities, such as Ghaziabad, Rohtak, Gurugram around Delhi.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How is the level of urbanisation measured?
cards.back: The level of urbanisation is measured in terms of percentage of urban population to total population.
cards.quote: The level of urbanisation is measured in terms of percentage of urban population to total population.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What was the level of urbanisation in India in 2011?
cards.back: The level of urbanisation in India in 2011 was 31.16 per cent, which is quite low in comparison to developed countries.
cards.quote: The level of urbanisation in India in 2011 was 31.16 per cent, which is quite low in comparison to developed countries.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Total urban population has increased ____ during the twentieth century.
cards.back: Total urban population has increased eleven-fold during the twentieth century.
cards.quote: Total urban population has increased eleven-fold during the twentieth century.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What are administrative towns?
cards.back: Towns supporting administrative headquarters of higher order are administrative towns, such as Chandigarh, New Delhi, Bhopal, Shillong, Guwahati, Imphal, Srinagar, Gandhinagar, Jaipur, Chennai, etc.
cards.quote: Towns supporting administrative headquarters of higher order are administrative towns, such as Chandigarh, New Delhi, Bhopal, Shillong, Guwahati, Imphal, Srinagar, Gandhinagar, Jaipur, Chennai, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Industrial towns: what is their prime motive force, and which are examples?
cards.back: Industries constitute prime motive force of these cities, such as Mumbai, Salem, Coimbatore, Modinagar, Jamshedpur, Hugli, Bhilai, etc.
cards.quote: Industries constitute prime motive force of these cities, such as Mumbai, Salem, Coimbatore, Modinagar, Jamshedpur, Hugli, Bhilai, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Transport cities: what two kinds are there, and which are examples?
cards.back: They may be ports primarily engaged in export and import activities such as Kandla, Cochin, Kozhikode, Vishakhapatnam, etc., or hubs of inland transport, such as Agra, Dhulia, Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Nagar, Itarsi, Katni, etc.
cards.quote: They may be ports primarily engaged in export and import activities such as Kandla, Cochin, Kozhikode, Vishakhapatnam, etc., or hubs of inland transport, such as Agra, Dhulia, Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Nagar, Itarsi, Katni, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which towns and cities are kept in the class of commercial towns?
cards.back: Towns and cities specialising in trade and commerce are kept in this class. Kolkata, Saharanpur, Satna, etc., are some examples.
cards.quote: Towns and cities specialising in trade and commerce are kept in this class. Kolkata, Saharanpur, Satna, etc., are some examples.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where have mining towns developed? Name examples.
cards.back: These towns have developed in mineral rich areas such as Raniganj, Jharia, Digboi, Ankaleshwar, Singrauli, etc.
cards.quote: These towns have developed in mineral rich areas such as Raniganj, Jharia, Digboi, Ankaleshwar, Singrauli, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name examples of garrison cantonment towns.
cards.back: These towns emerged as garrisson towns such as Ambala, Jalandhar, Mhow, Babina, Udhampur, etc.
cards.quote: These towns emerged as garrisson towns such as Ambala, Jalandhar, Mhow, Babina, Udhampur, etc.
cards.note: NCERT prints 'garrisson'; the usual spelling is garrison.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How did educational towns start? Name examples.
cards.back: Starting as centres of education, some of the towns have grown into major campus towns, such as Roorki, Varanasi, Aligarh, Pilani, Prayagraj, etc.
cards.quote: Starting as centres of education, some of the towns have grown into major campus towns, such as Roorki, Varanasi, Aligarh, Pilani, Prayagraj, etc.
cards.note: NCERT prints 'Roorki'; the usual spelling is Roorkee.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the religious and cultural towns of India.
cards.back: Varanasi, Mathura, Amritsar, Madurai, Puri, Ajmer, Pushkar, Tirupati, Kurukshetra, Haridwar, Ujjain came to prominence due to their religious/cultural significance.
cards.quote: Varanasi, Mathura, Amritsar, Madurai, Puri, Ajmer, Pushkar, Tirupati, Kurukshetra, Haridwar, Ujjain came to prominence due to their religious/cultural significance.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name examples of tourist towns of India.
cards.back: Nainital, Mussoorie, Shimla, Pachmarhi, Jodhpur, Jaisalmer, Udagamandalam (Ooty), Mount Abu are some of the tourist destinations.
cards.quote: Nainital, Mussoorie, Shimla, Pachmarhi, Jodhpur, Jaisalmer, Udagamandalam (Ooty), Mount Abu are some of the tourist destinations.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The cities are not ____ in their function. The functions change due to their ____ nature.
cards.back: The cities are not static in their function. The functions change due to their dynamic nature.
cards.quote: The cities are not static in their function. The functions change due to their dynamic nature.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Even specialised cities, as they grow into ____ become ____ wherein industry, business, administration, transport, etc., become important.
cards.back: Even specialised cities, as they grow into metropolises become multifunctional wherein industry, business, administration, transport, etc., become important.
cards.quote: Even specialised cities, as they grow into metropolises become multifunctional wherein industry, business, administration, transport, etc., become important.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What was India's total population in the 2011 Census, and its world rank by population?
cards.back: India is the second most populous country after China in the world with its total population of 1,210 million (2011).
cards.quote: India is the second most populous country after China in the world with its total population of 1,210 million (2011).

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: India's population is larger than the total population of ____ put together.
cards.back: India's population is larger than the total population of North America, South America and Australia put together.
cards.quote: India's population is larger than the total population of North America, South America and Australia put together.
blanks: North America, South America and Australia

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Population data are collected through Census operation held every ____ in our country.
cards.back: Population data are collected through Census operation held every 10 years in our country.
cards.quote: Population data are collected through Census operation held every 10 years in our country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The first population Census in India was conducted in ____ but its first complete Census was conducted only in ____.
cards.back: The first population Census in India was conducted in 1872 but its first complete Census was conducted only in 1881.
cards.quote: The first population Census in India was conducted in 1872 but its first complete Census was conducted only in 1881.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which state has the highest population in India, and which states follow?
cards.back: Uttar Pradesh has the highest population followed by Maharashtra, Bihar and West Bengal.
cards.quote: Uttar Pradesh has the highest population followed by Maharashtra, Bihar and West Bengal.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which ten states together account for about 76 per cent of India's population?
cards.back: U.P., Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh along with Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Karnataka and Gujarat, together account for about 76 per cent of the total population of the country.
cards.quote: U.P., Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh along with Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Karnataka and Gujarat, together account for about 76 per cent of the total population of the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name states with a very small population share despite a fairly large geographical area.
cards.back: On the other hand, share of population is very small in the states like Jammu & Kashmir (1.04%), Arunachal Pradesh (0.11%) and Uttarakhand (0.84%) inspite of theses states having fairly large geographical area.
cards.quote: On the other hand, share of population is very small in the states like Jammu & Kashmir (1.04%), Arunachal Pradesh (0.11%) and Uttarakhand (0.84%) inspite of theses states having fairly large geographical area.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which regions of India have a higher proportion of population than interior and hilly areas?
cards.back: Consequently, we observe that the North Indian Plains, deltas and Coastal Plains have higher proportion of population than the interior districts of southern and central Indian States, Himalayas, some of the north eastern and the western states.
cards.quote: Consequently, we observe that the North Indian Plains, deltas and Coastal Plains have higher proportion of population than the interior districts of southern and central Indian States, Himalayas, some of the north eastern and the western states.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What changes brought moderate to high population concentration in once thinly populated areas?
cards.back: However, development of irrigation (Rajasthan), availability of mineral and energy resources (Jharkhand) and development of transport network (Peninsular States) have resulted in moderate to high concentration of population in areas which were previously very thinly populated.
cards.quote: However, development of irrigation (Rajasthan), availability of mineral and energy resources (Jharkhand) and development of transport network (Peninsular States) have resulted in moderate to high concentration of population in areas which were previously very thinly populated.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the important socio-economic and historical factors of population distribution in India.
cards.back:
evolution of settled agriculture and agricultural development
pattern of human settlement
development of transport network, industrialisation and urbanisation
cards.quote: Among the socio-economic and historical factors of distribution of population, important ones are evolution of settled agriculture and agricultural development; pattern of human settlement; development of transport network, industrialisation and urbanisation.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Why do Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Pune, Ahmedabad, Chennai and Jaipur have high population concentration?
cards.back: the urban regions of Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Pune, Ahmedabad, Chennai and Jaipur have high concentration of population due to industrial development and urbanisation drawing a large numbers of rural-urban migrants.
cards.quote: the urban regions of Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Pune, Ahmedabad, Chennai and Jaipur have high concentration of population due to industrial development and urbanisation drawing a large numbers of rural-urban migrants.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is density of population?
cards.back: Density of population, is expressed as number of persons per unit area.
cards.quote: Density of population, is expressed as number of persons per unit area.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The density of population in India (2011) is ____ persons per sq km.
cards.back: The density of population in India (2011) is 382 persons per sq km.
cards.quote: The density of population in India (2011) is 382 persons per sq km.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How did India's density of population change between 1951 and 2011?
cards.back: There has been a steady increase of more than 200 persons per sq km over the last 50 years as the density of population increased from 117 persons/ sq km in 1951 to 382 persons/sq km in 2011.
cards.quote: There has been a steady increase of more than 200 persons per sq km over the last 50 years as the density of population increased from 117 persons/ sq km in 1951 to 382 persons/sq km in 2011.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What are the lowest and highest density among States/UTs in India (2011)?
cards.back: which ranges from as low as 17 persons per sq km in Arunachal Pradesh to 11,297 persons in the National Capital Territory of Delhi.
cards.quote: which ranges from as low as 17 persons per sq km in Arunachal Pradesh to 11,297 persons in the National Capital Territory of Delhi.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which northern and peninsular states have higher densities of population?
cards.back: Among the northern Indian States, Bihar (1102), West Bengal (1029) and and Uttar Pradesh (828) have higher densities, while Kerala (859) and Tamil Nadu (555) have higher densities among the peninsular Indian states.
cards.quote: Among the northern Indian States, Bihar (1102), West Bengal (1029) and and Uttar Pradesh (828) have higher densities, while Kerala (859) and Tamil Nadu (555) have higher densities among the peninsular Indian states.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which regions have relatively low densities and which have very high densities?
cards.back: The hill states of the Himalayan region and North eastern states of India (excluding Assam) have relatively low densities while the Union Territories (excluding Andaman and Nicobar islands) have very high densities of population
cards.quote: The hill states of the Himalayan region and North eastern states of India (excluding Assam) have relatively low densities while the Union Territories (excluding Andaman and Nicobar islands) have very high densities of population

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which two densities give a better insight into the human-land ratio than crude density?
cards.back: To get a better insight into the human-land ratio in terms of pressure of population on total cultivable land, the physiological and the agricultural densities should be found out
cards.quote: To get a better insight into the human-land ratio in terms of pressure of population on total cultivable land, the physiological and the agricultural densities should be found out

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Formula: physiological density
cards.back: Physiological density = total population / net cultivated area
cards.quote: Physiological density = total population / net cultivated area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Formula: agricultural density
cards.back: Agricultural density = total agricultural population / net cultivable area
cards.quote: Agricultural density = total agricultural population / net cultivable area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What does agricultural population include?
cards.back: Agricultural population includes cultivators and agricultural labourers and their family members.
cards.quote: Agricultural population includes cultivators and agricultural labourers and their family members.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is growth of population?
cards.back: Growth of population is the change in the number of people living in a particular area between two points of time.
cards.quote: Growth of population is the change in the number of people living in a particular area between two points of time.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Types: the two components of population growth
cards.back: natural and induced
cards.quote: Population growth has two components namely; natural and induced.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The annual growth rate of India's population is ____ per cent (2011).
cards.back: The annual growth rate of India's population is 1.64 per cent (2011).
cards.quote: The annual growth rate of India's population is 1.64 per cent (2011).

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is population doubling time?
cards.back: Population doubling time is the time taken by any population to double itself at its current annual growth rate.
cards.quote: Population doubling time is the time taken by any population to double itself at its current annual growth rate.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Phase I (1901-1921) of India's population growth: what is it called and why?
cards.back: Phase I : The period from 1901-1921 is referred to as a period of stagnant or stationary phase of growth of India's population, since in this period growth rate was very low, even recording a negative growth rate during 1911-1921.
cards.quote: Phase I : The period from 1901-1921 is referred to as a period of stagnant or stationary phase of growth of India's population, since in this period growth rate was very low, even recording a negative growth rate during 1911-1921.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Phase II (1921-1951): what is it called and what brought down mortality?
cards.back: The decades 1921-1951 are referred to as the period of steady population growth. An overall improvement in health and sanitation throughout the country brought down the mortality rate.
cards.quote: The decades 1921-1951 are referred to as the period of steady population growth. An overall improvement in health and sanitation throughout the country brought down the mortality rate.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Phase III (1951-1981): what is it called and what caused it?
cards.back: The decades 1951-1981 are referred to as the period of population explosion in India, which was caused by a rapid fall in the mortality rate but a high fertility rate of population in the country.
cards.quote: The decades 1951-1981 are referred to as the period of population explosion in India, which was caused by a rapid fall in the mortality rate but a high fertility rate of population in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Phase IV (post 1981): how does the growth rate behave, and why?
cards.back: In the post 1981 till present, the growth rate of country's population though remained high, has started slowing down gradually (Table 1.1). A downward trend of crude birth rate is held responsible for such a population growth.
cards.quote: In the post 1981 till present, the growth rate of country's population though remained high, has started slowing down gradually (Table 1.1). A downward trend of crude birth rate is held responsible for such a population growth.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What did the World Development Report project for India's population by 2025?
cards.back: it has been projected by World Development Report that population of India will touch 1,350 million by 2025.
cards.quote: it has been projected by World Development Report that population of India will touch 1,350 million by 2025.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which states show a low growth rate, not exceeding 20 per cent over the decade (1991-2001)?
cards.back: The States like Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Puducherry, and Goa show a low rate of growth not exceeding 20 per cent over the decade.
cards.quote: The States like Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Puducherry, and Goa show a low rate of growth not exceeding 20 per cent over the decade.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which state registered the lowest growth rate in the country, and what was it?
cards.back: Kerala registered the lowest growth rate (9.4) not only in this group of states but also in the country as a whole.
cards.quote: Kerala registered the lowest growth rate (9.4) not only in this group of states but also in the country as a whole.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which belt of states has relatively high growth rate than the southern states?
cards.back: A continuous belt of states from west to east in the north-west, north, and north central parts of the country has relatively high growth rate than the southern states.
cards.quote: A continuous belt of states from west to east in the north-west, north, and north central parts of the country has relatively high growth rate than the southern states.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How did growth rates of almost all States and UTs in 2001-2011 compare with 1991-2001?
cards.back: During 2001-2011, the growth rates of almost all States and Union Territories have registered a lower figure compared to the previous decade, namely, 1991-2001.
cards.quote: During 2001-2011, the growth rates of almost all States and Union Territories have registered a lower figure compared to the previous decade, namely, 1991-2001.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the share of adolescents (10-19 years) in India's population (2011)?
cards.back: At present the share of adolescents i.e., up to the age group of 10-19 years is about 20.9 per cent (2011), among which male adolescents constitute 52.7 per cent and female adolescents constitute 47.3 per cent.
cards.quote: At present the share of adolescents i.e., up to the age group of 10-19 years is about 20.9 per cent (2011), among which male adolescents constitute 52.7 per cent and female adolescents constitute 47.3 per cent.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How has the National Youth Policy (NYP-2014) defined 'youth'?
cards.back: The NYP-2014 has defined 'youth' as persons in the age group of 15-29 years.
cards.quote: The NYP-2014 has defined 'youth' as persons in the age group of 15-29 years.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is population composition?
cards.back: Population composition is a distinct field of study within population geography with a vast coverage of analysis of age and sex, place of residence, ethnic characteristics, tribes, language, religion, marital status, literacy and education, occupational characteristics, etc.
cards.quote: Population composition is a distinct field of study within population geography with a vast coverage of analysis of age and sex, place of residence, ethnic characteristics, tribes, language, religion, marital status, literacy and education, occupational characteristics, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How many villages does India have (Census 2011), and how many are inhabited?
cards.back: India has 640,867 villages according to the Census 2011 out of which 597,608 (93.2 per cent) are inhabited villages.
cards.quote: India has 640,867 villages according to the Census 2011 out of which 597,608 (93.2 per cent) are inhabited villages.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The growth rate of urban population has accelerated due to enhanced ____ and improvement in ____.
cards.back: The growth rate of urban population has accelerated due to enhanced economic development and improvement in health and hygienic conditions.
cards.quote: The growth rate of urban population has accelerated due to enhanced economic development and improvement in health and hygienic conditions.

cards.subject: geography
