cards.quote: In West Bengal farmers grow three crops of rice called ‘aus’, ‘aman’ and ‘boro’.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is India's share in world rice production, and its rank (2018)?
cards.back: India contributes 22.07 per cent of rice production in the world and ranked second after China in 2018.
cards.quote: India contributes 22.07 per cent of rice production in the world and ranked second after China in 2018.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which are the leading rice producing states in India?
cards.back: West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, and Punjab are the leading rice producing states in the country.
cards.quote: West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, and Punjab are the leading rice producing states in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Why is the rice yield high in Punjab and Haryana?
cards.back:
Genetically improved varieties of seed
relatively high usage of fertilizers and pesticides
lower levels of susceptibility of the crop to pests due to dry climatic conditions
cards.quote: Genetically improved varieties of seed, relatively high usage of fertilizers and pesticides and lower levels of susceptibility of the crop to pests due to dry climatic conditions

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Wheat is the ____ most important cereal crop in India after rice.
cards.back: Wheat is the second most important cereal crop in India after rice.
cards.quote: Wheat is the second most important cereal crop in India after rice.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What share of world wheat production does India produce (2017)?
cards.back: India produces about 12.8 per cent of total wheat production of world (2017).
cards.quote: India produces about 12.8 per cent of total wheat production of world (2017).

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where is about 85 per cent of the wheat area concentrated?
cards.back: About 85 per cent of total area under this crop is concentrated in north and central regions of the country i.e. Indo-Gangetic Plain, Malwa Plateau and Himalayas up to 2,700 m altitude.
cards.quote: About 85 per cent of total area under this crop is concentrated in north and central regions of the country i.e. Indo-Gangetic Plain, Malwa Plateau and Himalayas up to 2,700 m altitude.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which are the leading wheat producing states?
cards.back: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan are leading wheat producing states.
cards.quote: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan are leading wheat producing states.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where is the wheat yield very high?
cards.back: The yield level of wheat is very high (above 4,000 k.g. per ha) in Punjab and Haryana
cards.quote: The yield level of wheat is very high (above 4,000 k.g. per ha) in Punjab and Haryana

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What share of total cropped area does jowar (sorghum) alone account for?
cards.back: Among these, jowar or sorghum alone accounts for about 5.3 per cent of total cropped area.
cards.quote: Among these, jowar or sorghum alone accounts for about 5.3 per cent of total cropped area.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which state produces more than half of India's jowar?
cards.back: Maharashtra alone produces more than half of the total jowar production of the country.
cards.quote: Maharashtra alone produces more than half of the total jowar production of the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Bajra is sown in ____ climatic conditions in northwestern and western parts of the country.
cards.back: Bajra is sown in hot and dry climatic conditions in northwestern and western parts of the country.
cards.quote: Bajra is sown in hot and dry climatic conditions in northwestern and western parts of the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which are the leading bajra producing states?
cards.back: Leading producers of bajra are the states of Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and Haryana.
cards.quote: Leading producers of bajra are the states of Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and Haryana.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Pulses are a very important ingredient of vegetarian food as these are rich sources of ____.
cards.back: Pulses are a very important ingredient of vegetarian food as these are rich sources of proteins.
cards.quote: Pulses are a very important ingredient of vegetarian food as these are rich sources of proteins.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which are the main pulses cultivated in India?
cards.back: Gram and tur are the main pulses cultivated in India.
cards.quote: Gram and tur are the main pulses cultivated in India.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Gram is cultivated in which areas and in which season?
cards.back: Gram is cultivated in subtropical areas. It is mostly a rainfed crop cultivated during rabi season in central, western and northwestern parts of the country.
cards.quote: Gram is cultivated in subtropical areas. It is mostly a rainfed crop cultivated during rabi season in central, western and northwestern parts of the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: By which crop was gram displaced in Haryana, Punjab and northern Rajasthan?
cards.back: It has been displaced from the cropping pattern by wheat in Haryana, Punjab and northern Rajasthan following the green revolution.
cards.quote: It has been displaced from the cropping pattern by wheat in Haryana, Punjab and northern Rajasthan following the green revolution.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which is the second important pulse crop, and what is it also known as?
cards.back: Tur is the second important pulse crop in the country. It is also known as red gram or pigeon pea.
cards.quote: Tur is the second important pulse crop in the country. It is also known as red gram or pigeon pea.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How much of India's tur production does Maharashtra contribute?
cards.back: Maharashtra alone contributes about one-third of the total production of tur.
cards.quote: Maharashtra alone contributes about one-third of the total production of tur.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the main oilseed crops grown in India.
cards.back:
Groundnut
rapeseed and mustard
soyabean
sunflower
cards.quote: Groundnut, rapeseed and mustard, soyabean and sunflower are the main oilseed crops grown in India.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What share of world groundnut production does India produce (2018)?
cards.back: India produces about 18.8 per cent of the total groundnut production in the world (2018).
cards.quote: India produces about 18.8 per cent of the total groundnut production in the world (2018).

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which oilseeds do rapeseed and mustard comprise?
cards.back: Rapeseed and mustard comprise several oilseeds as rai, sarson, toria and taramira.
cards.quote: Rapeseed and mustard comprise several oilseeds as rai, sarson, toria and taramira.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where is soyabean mostly grown?
cards.back: Soyabean is mostly grown in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.
cards.quote: Soyabean is mostly grown in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the two main fibre crops grown in India.
cards.back:
Cotton
jute
cards.quote: Cotton and jute are two main fibre crops grown in India.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Cotton is a ____ crop grown in ____ season in semi-arid areas of the country.
cards.back: Cotton is a tropical crop grown in kharif season in semi-arid areas of the country.
cards.quote: Cotton is a tropical crop grown in kharif season in semi-arid areas of the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Cotton requires ____ during flowering stage.
cards.back: Cotton requires clear sky during flowering stage.
cards.quote: Cotton requires clear sky during flowering stage.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is India's rank in world cotton production?
cards.back: India ranks second in the world in the production of cotton after China.
cards.quote: India ranks second in the world in the production of cotton after China.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the three cotton growing areas of India.
cards.back:
parts of Punjab, Haryana and northern Rajasthan in north-west
Gujarat and Maharashtra in the west
plateaus of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu in south
cards.quote: There are three cotton growing areas, i.e. parts of Punjab, Haryana and northern Rajasthan in north-west, Gujarat and Maharashtra in the west and plateaus of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu in south.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What happened to India's cotton growing area at partition?
cards.back: India lost a large proportion of cotton growing area to Pakistan during partition.
cards.quote: India lost a large proportion of cotton growing area to Pakistan during partition.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is jute used for, and where is it a cash crop?
cards.back: Jute is used for making coarse cloth, bags, sacks and decorative items. It is a cash crop in West Bengal and adjoining eastern parts of the country.
cards.quote: Jute is used for making coarse cloth, bags, sacks and decorative items. It is a cash crop in West Bengal and adjoining eastern parts of the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is India's share in world jute production, and West Bengal's share in India's?
cards.back: At present, India produces about three-fifth of jute production of the world. West Bengal accounts for about three-fourth of the production in the country.
cards.quote: At present, India produces about three-fifth of jute production of the world. West Bengal accounts for about three-fourth of the production in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Sugarcane is a crop of which areas, and is it largely rainfed or irrigated in India?
cards.back: Sugarcane is a crop of tropical areas. Under rainfed conditions, it is cultivated in sub-humid and humid climates. But it is largely an irrigated crop in India.
cards.quote: Sugarcane is a crop of tropical areas. Under rainfed conditions, it is cultivated in sub-humid and humid climates. But it is largely an irrigated crop in India.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is India's rank and share in world sugarcane production (2018)?
cards.back: India was the second largest producer of sugarcane after Brazil in 2018. It accounts for about 19.7 per cent of the world production of sugarcane.
cards.quote: India was the second largest producer of sugarcane after Brazil in 2018. It accounts for about 19.7 per cent of the world production of sugarcane.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which state produces about two-fifth of India's sugarcane?
cards.back: Uttar Pradesh produces about two-fifth of sugarcane of the country.
cards.quote: Uttar Pradesh produces about two-fifth of sugarcane of the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Tea is a ____ crop used as beverage.
cards.back: Tea is a plantation crop used as beverage.
cards.quote: Tea is a plantation crop used as beverage.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: ____ tea leaves are fermented whereas ____ tea leaves are unfermented.
cards.back: Black tea leaves are fermented whereas green tea leaves are unfermented.
cards.quote: Black tea leaves are fermented whereas green tea leaves are unfermented.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Tea leaves have rich content of ____ and ____.
cards.back: Tea leaves have rich content of caffeine and tannin.
cards.quote: Tea leaves have rich content of caffeine and tannin.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: When and where did tea plantation start in India?
cards.back: In India, tea plantation started in 1840s in Brahmaputra valley of Assam which still is a major tea growing area in the country.
cards.quote: In India, tea plantation started in 1840s in Brahmaputra valley of Assam which still is a major tea growing area in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is India's share in world tea production (2018)?
cards.back: India is a leading producer of tea and accounts for about 21.22 per cent of total production in the world 2018.
cards.quote: India is a leading producer of tea and accounts for about 21.22 per cent of total production in the world 2018.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What share of India's tea area and production does Assam account for?
cards.back: Assam accounts for about 53.2 per cent of the total cropped area and contributes more than half of total production of tea in the country.
cards.quote: Assam accounts for about 53.2 per cent of the total cropped area and contributes more than half of total production of tea in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the three varieties of coffee.
cards.back:
arabica
robusta
liberica
cards.quote: There are three varieties of coffee i.e. arabica, robusta and liberica.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which variety of coffee does India mostly grow?
cards.back: India mostly grows superior quality coffee, arabica, which is in great demand in International market.
cards.quote: India mostly grows superior quality coffee, arabica, which is in great demand in International market.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where is coffee cultivated in India?
cards.back: Coffee is cultivated in the highlands of Western Ghats in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
cards.quote: Coffee is cultivated in the highlands of Western Ghats in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which state accounts for more than two-third of India's coffee production?
cards.back: Karnataka alone accounts for more than two-third of total production of coffee in the country.
cards.quote: Karnataka alone accounts for more than two-third of total production of coffee in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Indian agricultural economy was largely ____ in nature before Independence.
cards.back: Indian agricultural economy was largely subsistence in nature before Independence.
cards.quote: Indian agricultural economy was largely subsistence in nature before Independence.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: During partition about ____ of the irrigated land in undivided India went to Pakistan.
cards.back: During partition about one-third of the irrigated land in undivided India went to Pakistan.
cards.quote: During partition about one-third of the irrigated land in undivided India went to Pakistan.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: After Independence, how did the Government aim to increase foodgrains production? Give the three steps.
cards.back:
(i) switching over from cash crops to food crops
(ii) intensification of cropping over already cultivated land
(iii) increasing cultivated area by bringing cultivable and fallow land under plough
cards.quote: After Independence, the immediate goal of the Government was to increase foodgrains production by (i) switching over from cash crops to food crops; (ii) intensification of cropping over already cultivated land; and (iii) increasing cultivated area by bringing cultivable and fallow land under plough.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which two programmes were launched to overcome the stagnation in agricultural production?
cards.back: To overcome this problem, Intensive Agricultural District Programme (IADP) and Intensive Agricultural Area Programme (IAAP) were launched.
cards.quote: To overcome this problem, Intensive Agricultural District Programme (IADP) and Intensive Agricultural Area Programme (IAAP) were launched.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: But two consecutive ____ during mid-1960s resulted in food crisis in the country.
cards.back: But two consecutive droughts during mid-1960s resulted in food crisis in the country.
cards.quote: But two consecutive droughts during mid-1960s resulted in food crisis in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where were the new high yielding varieties (HYVs) of wheat and rice developed?
cards.back: New seed varieties of wheat (Mexico) and rice (Philippines) known as high yielding varieties (HYVs) were available for cultivation by mid-1960s.
cards.quote: New seed varieties of wheat (Mexico) and rice (Philippines) known as high yielding varieties (HYVs) were available for cultivation by mid-1960s.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where did India introduce the package technology of HYVs with chemical fertilisers?
cards.back: India took advantage of this and introduced package technology comprising HYVs, along with chemical fertilisers in irrigated areas of Punjab, Haryana, Western Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat.
cards.quote: India took advantage of this and introduced package technology comprising HYVs, along with chemical fertilisers in irrigated areas of Punjab, Haryana, Western Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Assured supply of soil moisture through ____ was a basic pre-requisite for the success of this new agricultural technology.
cards.back: Assured supply of soil moisture through irrigation was a basic pre-requisite for the success of this new agricultural technology.
cards.quote: Assured supply of soil moisture through irrigation was a basic pre-requisite for the success of this new agricultural technology.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the Green Revolution?
cards.back: This strategy of agricultural development paid dividends instantly and increased the foodgrains production at very fast rate. This spurt of agricultural growth came to be known as ‘Green Revolution’.
cards.quote: This strategy of agricultural development paid dividends instantly and increased the foodgrains production at very fast rate. This spurt of agricultural growth came to be known as ‘Green Revolution’.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What regional problem did the Green Revolution cause initially?
cards.back: But Green Revolution was initially confined to irrigated areas only. This led to regional disparities in agricultural development in the country till 1970s, after which the technology spread to the Eastern and Central parts of the country.
cards.quote: But Green Revolution was initially confined to irrigated areas only. This led to regional disparities in agricultural development in the country till 1970s, after which the technology spread to the Eastern and Central parts of the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: When did the Planning Commission initiate agro-climatic planning, and why?
cards.back: It initiated agro-climatic planning in 1988 to induce regionally balanced agricultural development in the country.
cards.quote: It initiated agro-climatic planning in 1988 to induce regionally balanced agricultural development in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Initiation of the policy of liberalisation and free market economy in ____ influenced the course of development of Indian agriculture.
cards.back: Initiation of the policy of liberalisation and free market economy in 1990s influenced the course of development of Indian agriculture.
cards.quote: Initiation of the policy of liberalisation and free market economy in 1990s influenced the course of development of Indian agriculture.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the aim of the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA)?
cards.back: National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture is to make agriculture more productive, sustainable, remunerative and climate resilient by promoting location specific integrated/composite farming systems and to conserve natural resources through appropriate soil and moisture conservation measures.
cards.quote: National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture is to make agriculture more productive, sustainable, remunerative and climate resilient by promoting location specific integrated/composite farming systems and to conserve natural resources through appropriate soil and moisture conservation measures.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Through which schemes does the Government promote organic farming?
cards.back: The Government has been promoting organic farming in the country through the scheme such as Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY) and Rashtriya Vikas Yojana (RKVY).
cards.quote: The Government has been promoting organic farming in the country through the scheme such as Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY) and Rashtriya Vikas Yojana (RKVY).

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Expansion of ____ has played a crucial role in enhancing agricultural output in the country.
cards.back: Expansion of irrigation has played a crucial role in enhancing agricultural output in the country.
cards.quote: Expansion of irrigation has played a crucial role in enhancing agricultural output in the country.

source.section: Growth of Agricultural Output and Technology

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Consumption of chemical fertilizers has increased by ____ since mid-sixties.
cards.back: Consumption of chemical fertilizers has increased by 15 times since mid-sixties.
cards.quote: Consumption of chemical fertilizers has increased by 15 times since mid-sixties.

source.section: Growth of Agricultural Output and Technology

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Since the high yielding varieties are highly susceptible to ____, the use of pesticides has increased significantly since 1960s.
cards.back: Since the high yielding varieties are highly susceptible to pests and diseases, the use of pesticides has increased significantly since 1960s.
cards.quote: Since the high yielding varieties are highly susceptible to pests and diseases, the use of pesticides has increased significantly since 1960s.

source.section: Growth of Agricultural Output and Technology

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How does poor performance of the south-west monsoon affect irrigation?
cards.back: Poor performance of south-west monsoon also adversely affects the supply of canal water for irrigation.
cards.quote: Poor performance of south-west monsoon also adversely affects the supply of canal water for irrigation.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How does India's crop yield compare with the international level?
cards.back: The yield of the crops in the country is low in comparison to the international level. Per hectare output of most of the crops such as rice, wheat, cotton and oilseeds in India is much lower than that of the U.S.A., Russia and Japan.
cards.quote: The yield of the crops in the country is low in comparison to the international level. Per hectare output of most of the crops such as rice, wheat, cotton and oilseeds in India is much lower than that of the U.S.A., Russia and Japan.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Why have modern inputs become unmanageable for marginal and small farmers?
cards.back: The inputs of modern agriculture are very expensive. This resource intensive approach has become unmanageable for marginal and small farmers as they have very meagre or no saving to invest in agriculture.
cards.quote: The inputs of modern agriculture are very expensive. This resource intensive approach has become unmanageable for marginal and small farmers as they have very meagre or no saving to invest in agriculture.

source.section: Constraints of Financial Resources and Indebtedness

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Why is there a lack of commercialisation among small farmers?
cards.back: A large number of farmers produce crops for self-consumption. These farmers do not have enough land resources to produce more than their requirement.
cards.quote: A large number of farmers produce crops for self-consumption. These farmers do not have enough land resources to produce more than their requirement.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the extent of seasonal unemployment in unirrigated tracts?
cards.back: There is a massive underemployment in the agricultural sector in India, particularly in the unirrigated tracts. In these areas, there is a seasonal unemployment ranging from 4 to 8 months.
cards.quote: There is a massive underemployment in the agricultural sector in India, particularly in the unirrigated tracts. In these areas, there is a seasonal unemployment ranging from 4 to 8 months.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the serious problem arising out of faulty irrigation and agricultural development strategy?
cards.back: One of the serious problems that arises out of faulty strategy of irrigation and agricultural development is degradation of land resources. This is serious because it may lead to depletion of soil fertility.
cards.quote: One of the serious problems that arises out of faulty strategy of irrigation and agricultural development is degradation of land resources. This is serious because it may lead to depletion of soil fertility.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What caused agricultural land in irrigated areas to lose fertility?
cards.back: A large tract of agricultural land has lost its fertility due to alkalisation and salinisation of soils and waterlogging.
cards.quote: A large tract of agricultural land has lost its fertility due to alkalisation and salinisation of soils and waterlogging.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What has obliterated the process of natural fertilization such as nitrogen fixation in irrigated areas?
cards.back: Leguminous crops have been displaced from the cropping pattern in the irrigated areas and duration of fallow has substantially reduced owing to multiple cropping. This has obliterated the process of natural fertilization such as nitrogen fixation.
cards.quote: Leguminous crops have been displaced from the cropping pattern in the irrigated areas and duration of fallow has substantially reduced owing to multiple cropping. This has obliterated the process of natural fertilization such as nitrogen fixation.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What kinds of degradation do rainfed areas in humid and semi-arid tropics experience?
cards.back: Rainfed areas in humid and semi-arid tropics also experience degradation of several types like soil erosion by water and wind erosion which are often induced by human activities.
cards.quote: Rainfed areas in humid and semi-arid tropics also experience degradation of several types like soil erosion by water and wind erosion which are often induced by human activities.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is a mineral?
cards.back: A mineral is a natural substance of organic or inorganic origin with definite chemical and physical properties.
cards.quote: A mineral is a natural substance of organic or inorganic origin with definite chemical and physical properties.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Types of mineral resources (on the basis of chemical and physical properties).
cards.back:
metallics
non-metallics
cards.quote: On the basis of chemical and physical properties, minerals may be grouped under two main categories of metallics and non-metallics

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Into which two kinds are metallic minerals further divided?
cards.back:
ferrous
non-ferrous
cards.quote: Metallic minerals are further divided into ferrous and non-ferrous metallic minerals.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Ferrous vs non-ferrous minerals: the difference on iron content.
cards.back: All those minerals which have iron content are ferrous such as iron ore itself and those which do not have iron content are non-ferrous such as copper, bauxite, etc.
cards.quote: All those minerals which have iron content are ferrous such as iron ore itself and those which do not have iron content are non-ferrous such as copper, bauxite, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Types of non-metallic minerals by origin.
cards.back: Non-metallic minerals are either organic in origin such as fossil fuels also known as mineral fuels which are derived from the buried animal and plant life such as coal and petroleum. Other type of non-metallic minerals are inorganic in origin such as mica, limestone and graphite, etc.
cards.quote: Non-metallic minerals are either organic in origin such as fossil fuels also known as mineral fuels which are derived from the buried animal and plant life such as coal and petroleum. Other type of non-metallic minerals are inorganic in origin such as mica, limestone and graphite, etc.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the three main characteristics of minerals.
cards.back:
unevenly distributed over space
inverse relationship in quality and quantity of minerals
all minerals are exhaustible over time
cards.quote: Minerals have certain characteristics. These are unevenly distributed over space. There is inverse relationship in quality and quantity of minerals i.e. good quality minerals are less in quantity as compared to low quality minerals. The third main characteristic is that all minerals are exhaustible over time.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: There is ____ in quality and quantity of minerals i.e. good quality minerals are less in quantity as compared to low quality minerals.
cards.back: There is inverse relationship in quality and quantity of minerals i.e. good quality minerals are less in quantity as compared to low quality minerals.
cards.quote: There is inverse relationship in quality and quantity of minerals i.e. good quality minerals are less in quantity as compared to low quality minerals.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Over ____ of coal reserves occur in the valleys of Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi and Godavari.
cards.back: Over 97 per cent of coal reserves occur in the valleys of Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi and Godavari.
cards.quote: Over 97 per cent of coal reserves occur in the valleys of Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi and Godavari.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where are the petroleum reserves of India located?
cards.back: Petroleum reserves are located in the sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High i.e. off-shore region in the Arabian Sea.
cards.quote: Petroleum reserves are located in the sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High i.e. off-shore region in the Arabian Sea.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where have new petroleum reserves been located in India?
cards.back: New reserves have been located in the Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins.
cards.quote: New reserves have been located in the Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Most of the major mineral resources occur to the east of a line linking ____.
cards.back: Most of the major mineral resources occur to the east of a line linking Mangaluru and Kanpur.
cards.quote: Most of the major mineral resources occur to the east of a line linking Mangaluru and Kanpur.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which regions does the North-Eastern Plateau mineral belt cover?
cards.back: This belt covers Chhotanagpur (Jharkhand), Odisha Plateau, West Bengal and parts of Chhattisgarh.
cards.quote: This belt covers Chhotanagpur (Jharkhand), Odisha Plateau, West Bengal and parts of Chhattisgarh.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the variety of minerals found in the North-Eastern Plateau Region.
cards.back: iron ore coal, manganese, bauxite, mica
cards.quote: It has variety of minerals viz. iron ore coal, manganese, bauxite, mica.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Over which areas does the South-Western Plateau mineral belt extend?
cards.back: This belt extends over Karnataka, Goa and contiguous Tamil Nadu uplands and Kerala.
cards.quote: This belt extends over Karnataka, Goa and contiguous Tamil Nadu uplands and Kerala.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Along which range does the North-Western mineral belt extend?
cards.back: This belt extends along Aravali in Rajasthan and part of Gujarat and minerals are associated with Dharwar system of rocks.
cards.quote: This belt extends along Aravali in Rajasthan and part of Gujarat and minerals are associated with Dharwar system of rocks.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which have been the major minerals of the North-Western mineral belt?
cards.back: Copper, zinc have been major minerals.
cards.quote: Copper, zinc have been major minerals.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Rajasthan is rich in ____ i.e. sandstone, granite, marble.
cards.back: Rajasthan is rich in building stones i.e. sandstone, granite, marble.
cards.quote: Rajasthan is rich in building stones i.e. sandstone, granite, marble.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Dolomite and limestone provide raw materials for ____ industry.
cards.back: Dolomite and limestone provide raw materials for cement industry.
cards.quote: Dolomite and limestone provide raw materials for cement industry.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which minerals are known to occur in the Himalayan mineral belt?
cards.back: The Himalayan belt is another mineral belt where copper, lead, zinc, cobalt and tungsten are known to occur.
cards.quote: The Himalayan belt is another mineral belt where copper, lead, zinc, cobalt and tungsten are known to occur.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: India has the largest reserve of which mineral in Asia?
cards.back: It has the largest reserve of iron ore in Asia.
cards.quote: It has the largest reserve of iron ore in Asia.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the two main types of iron ore found in India.
cards.back:
haematite
magnetite
cards.quote: The two main types of ore found in our country are haematite and magnetite.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The iron ore mines occur in close proximity to the ____ in the northeastern plateau region of the country which adds to their advantage.
cards.back: The iron ore mines occur in close proximity to the coal fields in the northeastern plateau region of the country which adds to their advantage.
cards.quote: The iron ore mines occur in close proximity to the coal fields in the northeastern plateau region of the country which adds to their advantage.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: In which States is about 95 per cent of India's iron ore reserve located?
cards.back: About 95 per cent of total reserves of iron ore is located in the States of Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
cards.quote: About 95 per cent of total reserves of iron ore is located in the States of Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where are Jharkhand's important iron ore mines Noamundi and Gua located?
cards.back: Most of the important mines such as Noamundi and Gua are located in Poorbi and Pashchimi Singhbhum districts.
cards.quote: Most of the important mines such as Noamundi and Gua are located in Poorbi and Pashchimi Singhbhum districts.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which iron ore mines in Durg are important in the country?
cards.back: Dalli, and Rajhara in Durg are the important mines of iron ore in the country.
cards.quote: Dalli, and Rajhara in Durg are the important mines of iron ore in the country.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: ____ is an important raw material for smelting of iron ore and also used for manufacturing ferro alloys.
cards.back: Manganese is an important raw material for smelting of iron ore and also used for manufacturing ferro alloys.
cards.quote: Manganese is an important raw material for smelting of iron ore and also used for manufacturing ferro alloys.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Manganese deposits are found in almost all geological formations, however, it is mainly associated with ____.
cards.back: Manganese deposits are found in almost all geological formations, however, it is mainly associated with Dharwar system.
cards.quote: Manganese deposits are found in almost all geological formations, however, it is mainly associated with Dharwar system.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which States are the leading producers of manganese?
cards.back: Madhya Pradesh and Odisha are the leading producers of Manganese.
cards.quote: Madhya Pradesh and Odisha are the leading producers of Manganese.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: India is poorly endowed with non-ferrous metallic minerals except ____.
cards.back: India is poorly endowed with non-ferrous metallic minerals except bauxite.
cards.quote: India is poorly endowed with non-ferrous metallic minerals except bauxite.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: ____ is the ore, which is used in manufacturing of aluminium.
cards.back: Bauxite is the ore, which is used in manufacturing of aluminium.
cards.quote: Bauxite is the ore, which is used in manufacturing of aluminium.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Bauxite is found mainly in ____ and is associated with ____
cards.back: Bauxite is found mainly in tertiary deposits and is associated with laterite rocks
cards.quote: Bauxite is found mainly in tertiary deposits and is associated with laterite rocks

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which State is the largest producer of bauxite?
cards.back: Odisha happens to be the largest producer of Bauxite.
cards.quote: Odisha happens to be the largest producer of Bauxite.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which are the leading bauxite producing areas of Odisha?
cards.back: Kalahandi and Sambalpur are the leading producers.
cards.quote: Kalahandi and Sambalpur are the leading producers.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Copper is an indispensable metal in the ____ for making wires, electric motors, transformers and generators.
cards.back: Copper is an indispensable metal in the electrical industry for making wires, electric motors, transformers and generators.
cards.quote: Copper is an indispensable metal in the electrical industry for making wires, electric motors, transformers and generators.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where do copper deposits mainly occur in India?
cards.back: The Copper deposits mainly occur in Singhbhum district in Jharkhand, Balaghat district in Madhya Pradesh and Jhunjhunu and Alwar districts in Rajasthan.
cards.quote: The Copper deposits mainly occur in Singhbhum district in Jharkhand, Balaghat district in Madhya Pradesh and Jhunjhunu and Alwar districts in Rajasthan.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Among the non-metallic minerals produced in India, ____ is the important one.
cards.back: Among the non-metallic minerals produced in India, mica is the important one.
cards.quote: Among the non-metallic minerals produced in India, mica is the important one.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which non-metallic minerals are extracted in India for local consumption?
cards.back: The other minerals extracted for local consumption are limestone, dolomite and phosphate.
cards.quote: The other minerals extracted for local consumption are limestone, dolomite and phosphate.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Mica is mainly used in the ____.
cards.back: Mica is mainly used in the electrical and electronic industries.
cards.quote: Mica is mainly used in the electrical and electronic industries.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where in Jharkhand is high quality mica obtained?
cards.back: In Jharkhand, high quality mica is obtained in a belt extending over a distance of about 150 km, in length and about 22 km, in width in lower Hazaribagh plateau.
cards.quote: In Jharkhand, high quality mica is obtained in a belt extending over a distance of about 150 km, in length and about 22 km, in width in lower Hazaribagh plateau.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which district of Andhra Pradesh produces the best quality mica?
cards.back: In Andhra Pradesh, Nellore district produces the best quality mica.
cards.quote: In Andhra Pradesh, Nellore district produces the best quality mica.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How far does the mica belt of Rajasthan extend?
cards.back: In Rajasthan, mica belt extends for about 320 kms from Jaipur to Bhilwara and around Udaipur.
cards.quote: In Rajasthan, mica belt extends for about 320 kms from Jaipur to Bhilwara and around Udaipur.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the conventional sources of energy.
cards.back: Mineral fuels like coal, petroleum and natural gas (known as fossil fuels), nuclear energy minerals, are the conventional sources of energy.
cards.quote: Mineral fuels like coal, petroleum and natural gas (known as fossil fuels), nuclear energy minerals, are the conventional sources of energy.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Coal is a one of the important minerals which is mainly used in the generation of ____ and ____.
cards.back: Coal is a one of the important minerals which is mainly used in the generation of thermal power and smelting of iron ore.
cards.quote: Coal is a one of the important minerals which is mainly used in the generation of thermal power and smelting of iron ore.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the two geological ages of the rock sequences in which coal mainly occurs.
cards.back:
Gondwana
tertiary deposits
cards.quote: Coal occurs in rock sequences mainly of two geological ages, namely Gondwana and tertiary deposits.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: About 80 per cent of the coal deposits in India is of ____ type and is of non-coking grade.
cards.back: About 80 per cent of the coal deposits in India is of bituminous type and is of non-coking grade.
cards.quote: About 80 per cent of the coal deposits in India is of bituminous type and is of non-coking grade.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where are the most important Gondwana coal fields of India located?
cards.back: The most important Gondwana coal fields of India are located in Damodar Valley.
cards.quote: The most important Gondwana coal fields of India are located in Damodar Valley.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the important coal fields of the Jharkhand-Bengal coal belt.
cards.back: They lie in Jharkhand-Bengal coal belt and the important coal fields in this region are Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura.
cards.quote: They lie in Jharkhand-Bengal coal belt and the important coal fields in this region are Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which is the largest coal field of India, followed by Raniganj?
cards.back: Jharia is the largest coal field followed by Raniganj.
cards.quote: Jharia is the largest coal field followed by Raniganj.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where do tertiary coals occur in India?
cards.back: Tertiary coals occur in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland.
cards.quote: Tertiary coals occur in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where does brown coal or lignite occur in India?
cards.back: Besides, the brown coal or lignite occur in the coastal areas of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Gujarat and Jammu and Kashmir.
cards.quote: Besides, the brown coal or lignite occur in the coastal areas of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Gujarat and Jammu and Kashmir.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is crude petroleum?
cards.back: Crude petroleum consists of hydrocarbons of liquid and gaseous states varying in chemical composition, colour and specific gravity.
cards.quote: Crude petroleum consists of hydrocarbons of liquid and gaseous states varying in chemical composition, colour and specific gravity.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Petroleum is referred to as ____ because of its scarcity and diversified uses.
cards.back: Petroleum is referred to as liquid gold because of its scarcity and diversified uses.
cards.quote: Petroleum is referred to as liquid gold because of its scarcity and diversified uses.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Crude petroleum occurs in ____ rocks of the ____ period.
cards.back: Crude petroleum occurs in sedimentary rocks of the tertiary period.
cards.quote: Crude petroleum occurs in sedimentary rocks of the tertiary period.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: When was the Oil and Natural Gas Commission set up, after which oil exploration was taken up systematically?
cards.back: Oil exploration and production was systematically taken up after the Oil and Natural Gas Commission was set up in 1956.
cards.quote: Oil exploration and production was systematically taken up after the Oil and Natural Gas Commission was set up in 1956.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which was the only oil producing region of India before 1956?
cards.back: Till then, Digboi in Assam was the only oil producing region but the scenario changed after 1956.
cards.quote: Till then, Digboi in Assam was the only oil producing region but the scenario changed after 1956.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: When was Mumbai High discovered and when did its production commence?
cards.back: Mumbai High which lies 160 km off Mumbai was discovered in 1973 and production commenced in 1976.
cards.quote: Mumbai High which lies 160 km off Mumbai was discovered in 1973 and production commenced in 1976.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which are the important oil producing areas of Assam?
cards.back: In Assam, Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran are important oil producing areas.
cards.quote: In Assam, Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran are important oil producing areas.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the major oilfields of Gujarat.
cards.back: The major oilfields of Gujarat are Ankaleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam, Kosamba and Lunej.
cards.quote: The major oilfields of Gujarat are Ankaleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam, Kosamba and Lunej.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Types of refineries in India, with an example of each.
cards.back: There are two types of refineries in India: (a) field-based and (b) market-based. Digboi is an example of field-based and Barauni is an example of market-based refinery.
cards.quote: There are two types of refineries in India: (a) field-based and (b) market-based. Digboi is an example of field-based and Barauni is an example of market-based refinery.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where are India's major natural gas reserves found?
cards.back: India's major gas reserves are found in the Mumbai High and allied fields along the west coast which are supplemented by finds in the Cambay basin.
cards.quote: India's major gas reserves are found in the Mumbai High and allied fields along the west coast which are supplemented by finds in the Cambay basin.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where have new natural gas reserves been discovered along the East Coast?
cards.back: Along the East Coast, new reserves of natural gas have been discovered in the Krishna-Godavari basin.
cards.quote: Along the East Coast, new reserves of natural gas have been discovered in the Krishna-Godavari basin.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the important minerals used for the generation of nuclear energy.
cards.back:
uranium
thorium
cards.quote: Important minerals used for the generation of nuclear energy are uranium and thorium.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: In which rocks do uranium deposits occur?
cards.back: Uranium deposits occur in the Dharwar rocks.
cards.quote: Uranium deposits occur in the Dharwar rocks.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: From which minerals is thorium mainly obtained?
cards.back: Thorium is mainly obtained from monazite and ilmenite in the beach sands along the coast of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
cards.quote: Thorium is mainly obtained from monazite and ilmenite in the beach sands along the coast of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where do the world's richest monazite deposits occur?
cards.back: World's richest monazite deposits occur in Palakkad and Kollam districts of Kerala, near Vishakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh and Mahanadi river delta in Odisha.
cards.quote: World's richest monazite deposits occur in Palakkad and Kollam districts of Kerala, near Vishakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh and Mahanadi river delta in Odisha.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Atomic Energy Commission was established in ____
cards.back: Atomic Energy Commission was established in 1948
cards.quote: Atomic Energy Commission was established in 1948

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the important nuclear power projects of India.
cards.back:
Tarapur (Maharashtra)
Rawatbhata near Kota (Rajasthan)
Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu)
Narora (Uttar Pradesh)
Kaiga (Karnataka)
Kakarapara (Gujarat)
cards.quote: The important nuclear power projects are Tarapur (Maharashtra), Rawatbhata near Kota (Rajasthan), Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu), Narora (Uttar Pradesh), Kaiga (Karnataka) and Kakarapara (Gujarat).

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is solar energy?
cards.back: Sun rays tapped in photovoltaic cells can be converted into energy, known as solar energy.
cards.quote: Sun rays tapped in photovoltaic cells can be converted into energy, known as solar energy.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the two processes considered very effective to tap solar energy.
cards.back:
photovoltaics
solar thermal technology
cards.quote: The two effective processes considered to be very effective to tap solar energy are photovoltaics and solar thermal technology.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Solar energy is ____ more effective than coal or oil based plants and ____ more effective than nuclear plants.
cards.back: Solar energy is 7 per cent more effective than coal or oil based plants and 10 per cent more effective than nuclear plants.
cards.quote: Solar energy is 7 per cent more effective than coal or oil based plants and 10 per cent more effective than nuclear plants.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which part of India has greater potential for solar energy development?
cards.back: The western part of India has greater potential for the development of solar energy in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
cards.quote: The western part of India has greater potential for the development of solar energy in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The kinetic energy of wind, through ____ is converted into electrical energy.
cards.back: The kinetic energy of wind, through turbines is converted into electrical energy.
cards.quote: The kinetic energy of wind, through turbines is converted into electrical energy.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: In which States do favourable conditions for wind energy exist?
cards.back: In Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka, favourable conditions for wind energy exist.
cards.quote: In Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka, favourable conditions for wind energy exist.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Along which coast of India do large tidal waves occur?
cards.back: Large tidal waves are known to occur along the west coast of India.
cards.quote: Large tidal waves are known to occur along the west coast of India.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where in India has a geothermal energy plant been commissioned?
cards.back: In India, a geothermal energy plant has been commissioned at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh.
cards.quote: In India, a geothermal energy plant has been commissioned at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is bio-energy?
cards.back: Bio-energy refers to energy derived from biological products which includes agricultural residues, municipal, industrial and other wastes.
cards.quote: Bio-energy refers to energy derived from biological products which includes agricultural residues, municipal, industrial and other wastes.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which project in Delhi converts municipal waste into energy?
cards.back: One such project converting municipal waste into energy is Okhla in Delhi.
cards.quote: One such project converting municipal waste into energy is Okhla in Delhi.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: In this chapter, planning is used with reference to which process?
cards.back: it has been used with reference to the process of economic development.
cards.quote: Though it is a very broad term, in this chapter, it has been used with reference to the process of economic development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Types of approaches to planning.
cards.back:
sectoral planning
regional planning
cards.quote: Generally, there are two approaches to planning, i.e., sectoral planning and regional planning.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is sectoral planning?
cards.back: Sectoral planning means formulation and implementation of the sets of schemes or programmes aimed at development of various sectors of the economy, such as agriculture, irrigation, manufacturing, power, construction, transport, communication, social infrastructure and services.
cards.quote: Sectoral planning means formulation and implementation of the sets of schemes or programmes aimed at development of various sectors of the economy, such as agriculture, irrigation, manufacturing, power, construction, transport, communication, social infrastructure and services.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is regional planning?
cards.back: This uneven pattern of development over space necessitates that the planners have a spatial perspective and draw the plans to reduce regional imbalance in development. This type of planning is termed as regional planning.
cards.quote: This uneven pattern of development over space necessitates that the planners have a spatial perspective and draw the plans to reduce regional imbalance in development. This type of planning is termed as regional planning.
cards.note: Regional planning aims to reduce uneven development between areas.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: When was the NITI Aayog formed?
cards.back: On 1 January 2015, the NITI Aayog was formed.
cards.quote: On 1 January 2015, the NITI Aayog was formed.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: With what objective has NITI Aayog been set up?
cards.back: NITI Aayog has been set up with the objective of involving the states in economic policy making for India for providing strategic and technical advice to the Central and State governments.
cards.quote: NITI Aayog has been set up with the objective of involving the states in economic policy making for India for providing strategic and technical advice to the Central and State governments.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: India adopted centralised planning after Independence, but subsequently, it graduated into ____ multi-level planning.
cards.back: India adopted centralised planning after Independence, but subsequently, it graduated into decentralised multi-level planning.
cards.quote: India adopted centralised planning after Independence, but subsequently, it graduated into decentralised multi-level planning.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The planning process has to take special care of those areas which have remained ____.
cards.back: The planning process has to take special care of those areas which have remained economically backward.
cards.quote: The planning process has to take special care of those areas which have remained economically backward.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the examples of programmes directed towards the development of target areas.
cards.back:
Command Area Development Programme
Drought Prone Area Development Programme
Desert Development Programme
Hill Area Development Programme
cards.quote: Some of the examples of programmes directed towards the development of target areas are Command Area Development Programme, Drought Prone Area Development Programme, Desert Development Programme, Hill Area Development Programme.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which agencies are examples of target group programmes?
cards.back: The Small Farmers Development Agency (SFDA) and Marginal Farmers Development Agency (MFDA)
cards.quote: The Small Farmers Development Agency (SFDA) and Marginal Farmers Development Agency (MFDA) which are the examples of target group programme.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: In the 8th Five Year Plan, special area programmes were designed to develop infrastructure in which areas?
cards.back: hill areas, north-eastern states, tribal areas and backward areas
cards.quote: In the 8th Five Year Plan special area programmes were designed to develop infrastructure in hill areas, north-eastern states, tribal areas and backward areas.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: During which Five Year Plan were Hill Area Development Programmes initiated?
cards.back: Hill Area Development Programmes were initiated during the Fifth Five Year Plan covering 15 districts
cards.quote: Hill Area Development Programmes were initiated during the Fifth Five Year Plan covering 15 districts comprising all the hilly districts of Uttar Pradesh (present Uttarakhand), Mikir Hill and North Cachar hills of Assam, Darjeeling district of West Bengal and Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the hill areas covered at the start of the Hill Area Development Programme.
cards.back:
all the hilly districts of Uttar Pradesh (present Uttarakhand)
Mikir Hill and North Cachar hills of Assam
Darjeeling district of West Bengal
Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu
cards.quote: Hill Area Development Programmes were initiated during the Fifth Five Year Plan covering 15 districts comprising all the hilly districts of Uttar Pradesh (present Uttarakhand), Mikir Hill and North Cachar hills of Assam, Darjeeling district of West Bengal and Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: In 1981, which hill areas did the National Committee on the Development of Backward Area say should be treated as backward?
cards.back: all the hill areas in the country having height above 600 m and not covered under tribal sub-plan
cards.quote: The National Committee on the Development of Backward Area in 1981 recommended that all the hill areas in the country having height above 600 m and not covered under tribal sub-plan be treated as backward hill areas.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Hill Area Development Programmes harness indigenous resources through development of what?
cards.back:
horticulture
plantation
agriculture
animal husbandry
poultry
forestry
small-scale and village industry
cards.quote: These programmes aimed at harnessing the indigenous resources of the hill areas through development of horticulture, plantation, agriculture, animal husbandry, poultry, forestry and small-scale and village industry.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Drought Prone Area Programme: when was it initiated and with what objectives?
cards.back: This programme was initiated during the Fourth Five Year Plan with the objectives of providing employment to the people in drought-prone areas and creating productive assets.
cards.quote: This programme was initiated during the Fourth Five Year Plan with the objectives of providing employment to the people in drought-prone areas and creating productive assets.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What did the Drought Prone Area Programme initially emphasise?
cards.back: the construction of labour-intensive civil works
cards.quote: Initially, this programme laid emphasis on the construction of labour-intensive civil works.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What did the Drought Prone Area Programme later emphasise?
cards.back:
irrigation projects
land development programmes
afforestation
grassland development
creation of basic rural infrastructure, such as electricity, roads, market, credit and services
cards.quote: But later on, it emphasised on irrigation projects, land development programmes, afforestation, grassland development and creation of basic rural infrastructure, such as electricity, roads, market, credit and services.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The other strategies of development of these areas include adoption of integrated ____ development approach at the micro-level.
cards.back: The other strategies of development of these areas include adoption of integrated watershed development approach at the micro-level.
cards.quote: The other strategies of development of these areas include adoption of integrated watershed development approach at the micro-level.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The restoration of ____ between water, soil, plants, and human and animal population should be a basic consideration
cards.back: The restoration of ecological balance between water, soil, plants, and human and animal population should be a basic consideration
cards.quote: The restoration of ecological balance between water, soil, plants, and human and animal population should be a basic consideration

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How many districts did the Planning Commission (1967) identify as prone to drought?
cards.back: The Planning Commission of India (1967) identified 67 districts (entire or partly) of the country prone to drought.
cards.quote: The Planning Commission of India (1967) identified 67 districts (entire or partly) of the country prone to drought.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which commission introduced the criterion of 30 per cent irrigated area to demarcate drought-prone areas?
cards.back: The Irrigation Commission (1972) introduced the criterion of 30 per cent irrigated area and demarcated the drought-prone areas.
cards.quote: The Irrigation Commission (1972) introduced the criterion of 30 per cent irrigated area and demarcated the drought-prone areas.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which drought-prone areas are largely protected due to the spread of irrigation?
cards.back: Punjab, Haryana and north-Rajasthan
cards.quote: The drought-prone areas of Punjab, Haryana and north-Rajasthan are largely protected due to spread of irrigation in these regions.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which tehsils and district make up the Bharmaur tribal area?
cards.back: Bharmaur tribal area comprises Bharmaur and Holi tehsils of Chamba district of Himachal Pradesh.
cards.quote: Bharmaur tribal area comprises Bharmaur and Holi tehsils of Chamba district of Himachal Pradesh.

source.section: Case Study: Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which tribal community inhabits the Bharmaur region?
cards.back: Bharmaur is inhabited by 'Gaddi', a tribal community
cards.quote: Bharmaur is inhabited by 'Gaddi', a tribal community who have maintained a distinct identity in the Himalayan region as they practised transhumance and conversed through Gaddiali dialect.

source.section: Case Study: Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: On what is the economy of Bharmaur largely based?
cards.back: The economy is largely based on agriculture and allied activities such as sheep and goat rearing.
cards.quote: The economy is largely based on agriculture and allied activities such as sheep and goat rearing.

source.section: Case Study: Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: When was the tribal sub-plan introduced and how many ITDPs were designated in Himachal Pradesh?
cards.back: the tribal sub-plan was introduced in 1974 and Bharmaur was designated as one of the five Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDP) in Himachal Pradesh.
cards.quote: the tribal sub-plan was introduced in 1974 and Bharmaur was designated as one of the five Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDP) in Himachal Pradesh.

source.section: Case Study: Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the sectors given the highest priority by the Bharmaur area development plan.
cards.back:
transport and communications
agriculture and allied activities
social and community services
cards.quote: This plan laid the highest priority on development of transport and communications, agriculture and allied activities, and social and community services.

source.section: Case Study: Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Name the infrastructure developed as the most significant contribution of the tribal sub-plan in Bharmaur.
cards.back:
schools
healthcare facilities
potable water
roads
communications
electricity
cards.quote: The most significant contribution of tribal sub-plan in Bharmaur region is the development of infrastructure in terms of schools, healthcare facilities, potable water, roads, communications and electricity.

source.section: Case Study: Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What are the social benefits of ITDP in the Bharmaur tribal region?
cards.back:
tremendous increase in literacy rate
improvement in sex ratio
decline in child marriage
cards.quote: The social benefits derived from ITDP include tremendous increase in literacy rate, improvement in sex ratio and decline in child marriage.

source.section: Case Study: Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: By how much did female literacy in Bharmaur rise between 1971 and 2011?
cards.back: The female literacy rate in the region increased from 1.88 per cent in 1971 to 65 per cent in 2011.
cards.quote: The female literacy rate in the region increased from 1.88 per cent in 1971 to 65 per cent in 2011.

source.section: Case Study: Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is development, as NCERT describes it?
cards.back: Hence, development is a multi-dimensional concept and signifies the positive, irreversible transformation of the economy, society and environment.
cards.quote: Hence, development is a multi-dimensional concept and signifies the positive, irreversible transformation of the economy, society and environment.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: In the post World War II era, the concept of development was synonymous to ____
cards.back: In the post World War II era, the concept of development was synonymous to economic growth
cards.quote: In the post World War II era, the concept of development was synonymous to economic growth

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which phrases were incorporated in the definition of development in the 1970s?
cards.back: redistribution with growth and growth and equity
cards.quote: So, in 1970s, the phrases such as redistribution with growth and growth and equity were incorporated in the definition of development.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: By the 1980s, what did the concept of development encapsulate?
cards.back: wide-spread improvement in social as well as material wellbeing of all in a society
cards.quote: By 1980s, development emerged as a concept encapsulating wide-spread improvement in social as well as material wellbeing of all in a society.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: When did the notion of sustainable development emerge, and in response to what?
cards.back: The notion of sustainable development emerged in the wake of general rise in the awareness of environmental issues in the late 1960s in Western World.
cards.quote: The notion of sustainable development emerged in the wake of general rise in the awareness of environmental issues in the late 1960s in Western World.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which two books raised fear among environmentalists about environmental issues?
cards.back: The publication of 'The Population Bomb' by Ehrlich in 1968 and 'The Limits to Growth' by Meadows and others in 1972 further raised the level of fear among environmentalists in particular and people in general.
cards.quote: The publication of 'The Population Bomb' by Ehrlich in 1968 and 'The Limits to Growth' by Meadows and others in 1972 further raised the level of fear among environmentalists in particular and people in general.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Who headed the World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED)?
cards.back: a World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED) headed by the Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland
cards.quote: Concerned with the growing opinion of world community on the environmental issues, the United Nations established a World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED) headed by the Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which report did the Brundtland Commission give in 1987?
cards.back: The Commission gave its report (also known as Brundtland Report) entitled 'Our Common Future' in 1987.
cards.quote: The Commission gave its report (also known as Brundtland Report) entitled 'Our Common Future' in 1987.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Define sustainable development (Brundtland Report, 1987).
cards.back: development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
cards.quote: The report defines sustainable development as a "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs."

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Aspects of development that sustainable development takes care of.
cards.back:
ecological
social
economic
cards.quote: Sustainable development takes care of ecological, social and economic aspects of development during the present times

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What does sustainable development plead for?
cards.back: for conservation of resources to enable the future generations to use these resources.
cards.quote: for conservation of resources to enable the future generations to use these resources.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: By what name was the Indira Gandhi Canal previously known?
cards.back: previously known as the Rajasthan Canal
cards.quote: Indira Gandhi Canal, previously known as the Rajasthan Canal, is one of the largest canal systems in India.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Who conceived the Indira Gandhi Canal project, and when was it launched?
cards.back: Conceived by Kanwar Sain in 1948, the canal project was launched on 31 March, 1958.
cards.quote: Conceived by Kanwar Sain in 1948, the canal project was launched on 31 March, 1958.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Where does the Indira Gandhi Canal originate and where does it run?
cards.back: The canal originates at Harike barrage in Punjab and runs parallel to Pakistan border at an average distance of 40 km in Thar Desert (Marusthali) of Rajasthan.
cards.quote: The canal originates at Harike barrage in Punjab and runs parallel to Pakistan border at an average distance of 40 km in Thar Desert (Marusthali) of Rajasthan.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the total planned length and culturable command area of the Indira Gandhi Canal system?
cards.back: The total planned length of the system is 9,060 km catering to the irrigation needs of a total culturable command area of 19.63 lakh hectares.
cards.quote: The total planned length of the system is 9,060 km catering to the irrigation needs of a total culturable command area of 19.63 lakh hectares.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which districts lie in the command area of Stage-I of the Indira Gandhi Canal?
cards.back: Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and northern part of Bikaner districts
cards.quote: The command area of Stage-I lies in Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and northern part of Bikaner districts.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which districts does the command area of Stage-II cover, and how large is it?
cards.back: The command area of Stage-II is spread over Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur and Churu districts covering culturable command area of 14.10 lakh ha.
cards.quote: The command area of Stage-II is spread over Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur and Churu districts covering culturable command area of 14.10 lakh ha.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What happens in a lift canal?
cards.back: In the lift canal, the water is lifted up to make it to flow against the slope of the land.
cards.quote: In the lift canal, the water is lifted up to make it to flow against the slope of the land.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: On which bank of the main canal do the lift canals originate, and what are the right-bank canals?
cards.back: All the lift canals of Indira Gandhi Canal system originate at the left bank of main canal while all the canals on the right bank of main canal are flow channels.
cards.quote: All the lift canals of Indira Gandhi Canal system originate at the left bank of main canal while all the canals on the right bank of main canal are flow channels.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What are the positive environmental impacts of canal irrigation in the Indira Gandhi Canal command area?
cards.back:
resulted in greening the land
reducing wind erosion and siltation of canal systems
cards.quote: The availability of soil moisture for a longer period of time and various afforestation and pasture development programmes under CAD have resulted in greening the land. This has also helped in reducing wind erosion and siltation of canal systems.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What has the spread of canal irrigation led to in the region?
cards.back: increase in cultivated area and intensity of cropping
cards.quote: Spread of canal irrigation has led to increase in cultivated area and intensity of cropping.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Which traditional crops have been replaced, and by which crops, in the canal command area?
cards.back: The traditional crops sown in the area, gram, bajra and jowar have been replaced by wheat, cotton, groundnut and rice.
cards.quote: The traditional crops sown in the area, gram, bajra and jowar have been replaced by wheat, cotton, groundnut and rice.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: But the intensive irrigation and excessive use of water has led to the emergence of twin environmental problems of ____ and ____.
cards.back: But the intensive irrigation and excessive use of water has led to the emergence of twin environmental problems of waterlogging and soil salinity.
cards.quote: But the intensive irrigation and excessive use of water has led to the emergence of twin environmental problems of waterlogging and soil salinity.

source.section: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The first requirement is strict implementation of ____.
cards.back: The first requirement is strict implementation of water management policy.
cards.quote: The first requirement is strict implementation of water management policy.

source.section: Measures for Promotion of Sustainable Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: In general, the cropping pattern shall not include ____.
cards.back: In general, the cropping pattern shall not include water intensive crops.
cards.quote: In general, the cropping pattern shall not include water intensive crops.

source.section: Measures for Promotion of Sustainable Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: ____ system (equal distribution of canal water in the command area of outlet)
cards.back: warabandi system (equal distribution of canal water in the command area of outlet)
cards.quote: warabandi system (equal distribution of canal water in the command area of outlet)

source.section: Measures for Promotion of Sustainable Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: The eco-development through afforestation, ____ and pasture development is necessary particularly in the fragile environment of Stage-II.
cards.back: The eco-development through afforestation, shelterbelt plantation and pasture development is necessary particularly in the fragile environment of Stage-II.
cards.quote: The eco-development through afforestation, shelterbelt plantation and pasture development is necessary particularly in the fragile environment of Stage-II.

source.section: Measures for Promotion of Sustainable Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How can social sustainability in the Indira Gandhi Canal command area be achieved?
cards.back: the land allottees having poor economic background are provided adequate financial and institutional support for cultivation of land.
cards.quote: The social sustainability in the region can be achieved only if the land allottees having poor economic background are provided adequate financial and institutional support for cultivation of land.

source.section: Measures for Promotion of Sustainable Development

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Whose remark on Asia: "Asia has many places where people are few and few place where people are very many"?
cards.back: The remark of George B. Cressey about the population of Asia that "Asia has many places where people are few and few place where people are very many" is true about the pattern of population distribution of the world also.
cards.quote: The remark of George B. Cressey about the population of Asia that "Asia has many places where people are few and few place where people are very many" is true about the pattern of population distribution of the world also.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: How many people did the world record at the beginning of the 21st century?
cards.back: The world at the beginning of 21st century recorded the presence of over 6 billion population.
cards.quote: The world at the beginning of 21st century recorded the presence of over 6 billion population.

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is population distribution?
cards.back: The term population distribution refers to the way people are spaced over the earth's surface.
cards.quote: The term population distribution refers to the way people are spaced over the earth's surface.

source.section: Patterns of Population Distribution in the World

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: Broadly, ____ of the world population lives in about ____ of its land area.
cards.back: Broadly, 90 per cent of the world population lives in about 10 per cent of its land area.
cards.quote: Broadly, 90 per cent of the world population lives in about 10 per cent of its land area.

source.section: Patterns of Population Distribution in the World

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What share of world population do the 10 most populous countries hold, and how many are in Asia?
cards.back: The 10 most populous countries of the world contribute about 60 per cent of the world's population. Of these 10 countries, 6 are located in Asia.
cards.quote: The 10 most populous countries of the world contribute about 60 per cent of the world's population. Of these 10 countries, 6 are located in Asia.

source.section: Patterns of Population Distribution in the World

cards.subject: geography
cards.front: What is the density of population, and in what unit is it usually measured?
